**E) The dollar's devaluation under the Gold Reserve Act represented a rise in the gold price of exactly $14.33 per ounce.**

Paragraph (7) moves the dollar gold price from $20.67 to $35.00. Subtract: 35.00 − 20.67 = 14.33. The statement's "exactly $14.33" is the correct arithmetic difference between those stated prices.

$35.00 − $20.67 = $14.33, so the magnitude claim is **true**.
highlights: abandoned the gold standard permanently in September of that year, and the pound's value fell by approximately 25%
approximately 25% against gold-backed currencies
close to 40% of total world gold output by the early 1900s
By 1936, when France, the last major holdout, also abandoned gold convertibility
devalued the dollar from $20.67 to $35.00 per ounce of gold

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.exam_title: Grammar Rules (New Sentences, Anchored in Gold Standard Vocabulary)
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the gold standard passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "Had Britain not returned to gold at the pre-war parity, Keynes's predicted deflation might have been avoided."
"The committee insisted that convertibility is restored before the end of the year."
"The number of countries abandoning gold convertibility continue to rise throughout the 1930s."
"Neither the Bank of England nor other central banks were fully able to prevent the crisis."
"Having suspended convertibility, the currency's value was immediately devalued by the government."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Had Britain not returned to gold at the pre-war parity, Keynes's predicted deflation might have been avoided."**

This is a well-formed third conditional with subject–auxiliary inversion: Had + subject + past participle in the if-clause, and a modal perfect ("might have been avoided") in the result clause. No auxiliary is missing, and the participle/modal pairing fits a counterfactual past.

Inverted Had + past participle with modal perfect is the standard third-conditional pattern, so the sentence is **true**.

**B) "The committee insisted that convertibility is restored before the end of the year."**

After insist + that, formal exam English wants the mandative subjunctive — base form "be," not indicative "is." Repair to "The committee insisted that convertibility be restored before the end of the year."

**Trap:** "Is restored" looks like an ordinary present after that-clause verbs that actually demand the bare subjunctive.

Insist that requires the base subjunctive, so the line is **false** — "…that convertibility be restored…."

**C) "The number of countries abandoning gold convertibility continue to rise throughout the 1930s."**

"The number of" is a singular subject, so the verb must be singular: "continues," not "continue." Repair to "The number of countries abandoning gold convertibility continues to rise throughout the 1930s."

**Trap:** The nearby plural "countries" tempts agreement with the wrong noun.

Subject–verb agreement fails with "the number… continue," so this is **false** — use "continues."

**D) "Neither the Bank of England nor other central banks were fully able to prevent the crisis."**

With neither…nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. Here "other central banks" is plural, so "were" is the right choice. The correlative structure is clean and the agreement rule is applied correctly.

Nearest-subject agreement with plural "central banks" justifies "were," so the sentence is **true**.

**E) "Having suspended convertibility, the currency's value was immediately devalued by the government."**

The opening participle "Having suspended convertibility" must modify the subject that did the suspending. As written, the subject is "the currency's value," which cannot suspend convertibility — a classic dangling modifier. Repair by making the government the subject: "Having suspended convertibility, the government immediately devalued the currency."

**Trap:** A passive main clause after an active participle often leaves the agent orphaned.

The dangling participle attaches the wrong actor, so the line is **false** — restore a human/institutional subject for the -ing phrase.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "No sooner had the pound fallen than confidence in sterling began to weaken further."
"The Bank of England, along with several allied institutions, were coordinating discount rates."
"Each of the major powers have committed to a fixed gold rate by 1900."
"By the time France abandoned gold in 1936, the classical system will have already collapsed."
"The reserves, which were held partly in foreign currencies, exposed the system to cascading crises."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "No sooner had the pound fallen than confidence in sterling began to weaken further."**

"No sooner…than" correctly triggers inversion: auxiliary Had + subject + past participle, then than + a simple-past follow-on. The sequence (fall, then further weakening) sits in the expected past-perfect → past-simple frame.

No sooner + inversion + than is formed correctly here, so the sentence is **true**.

**B) "The Bank of England, along with several allied institutions, were coordinating discount rates."**

"Along with several allied institutions" is a parenthetical add-on; the grammatical subject remains singular "The Bank of England," so the verb should be "was coordinating," not "were." Repair: "The Bank of England, along with several allied institutions, was coordinating discount rates."

**Trap:** Material after along with/as well as does not make a plural subject.

Singular Bank of England needs "was," so "were" makes the line **false**.

**C) "Each of the major powers have committed to a fixed gold rate by 1900."**

"Each of" takes a singular verb even when a plural noun follows. Prefer "has committed," not "have." Repair: "Each of the major powers has committed to a fixed gold rate by 1900."

**Trap:** "Powers" looks plural, but each of still governs singular agreement.

Each of + have breaks singular agreement, so the sentence is **false** — "has committed."

**D) "By the time France abandoned gold in 1936, the classical system will have already collapsed."**

"By the time France abandoned…" anchors a past viewpoint, so the main clause needs past perfect ("had already collapsed"), not future perfect ("will have already collapsed"). Future perfect belongs with a still-ahead deadline, not a finished 1936 narrative.

**Trap:** "By the time" can tempt will have even when the time clause is already past.

A past by-the-time frame rejects will have, so this is **false** — "…the classical system had already collapsed."

**E) "The reserves, which were held partly in foreign currencies, exposed the system to cascading crises."**

The non-restrictive which-clause correctly modifies plural "reserves," and "were held" agrees with that plural noun. The main verb "exposed" also matches the plural subject. Relative-clause agreement and punctuation are in order.

Plural reserves + "which were held" agree cleanly, so the sentence is **true**.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "Historians remain divided as to whether the collapse resulted primarily from wartime disruption."
"Despite of the theoretical self-correcting mechanism, the system depended on informal cooperation."
"Whoever restores convertibility at an overvalued rate risks forcing painful deflation on the economy."
"Churchill denied having fully considered the deflationary consequences of the decision."
"There is several factors that explain the system's stability before 1914."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Historians remain divided as to whether the collapse resulted primarily from wartime disruption."**

"Remain divided as to whether…" correctly introduces an embedded yes/no question after as to. Tense and subject–verb agreement are fine, and whether (not if) is a natural choice after a prepositional as to.

The as to whether structure is well formed, so the sentence is **true**.

**B) "Despite of the theoretical self-correcting mechanism, the system depended on informal cooperation."**

Despite never takes of; that of belongs with in spite of. Repair to "Despite the theoretical self-correcting mechanism…" or "In spite of the theoretical self-correcting mechanism…."

**Trap:** Despite / in spite of get blended into the ungrammatical "despite of."

"Despite of" is not standard English, so the line is **false** — drop of or switch to in spite of.

**C) "Whoever restores convertibility at an overvalued rate risks forcing painful deflation on the economy."**

Whoever correctly heads a subject noun clause, and the main verb "risks" agrees with that singular -ever subject. "Risks forcing" (risk + -ing) is the expected pattern after risk.

Whoever + singular risks + -ing is grammatical, so the sentence is **true**.

**D) "Churchill denied having fully considered the deflationary consequences of the decision."**

After deny, a perfect gerund ("having fully considered") correctly marks an earlier completed action the speaker rejects. Word order and aspect are appropriate for denying a prior consideration.

Denied + perfect gerund is the right pattern here, so the wording is **true**.

**E) "There is several factors that explain the system's stability before 1914."**

Existential there must agree with the notional subject that follows. "Several factors" is plural, so the verb must be "are," not "is." Repair: "There are several factors that explain the system's stability before 1914."

**Trap:** There is feels default until the plural noun after it is noticed.

Plural factors need There are, so "There is several" is **false**.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly written, using a word or phrase echoing the passage's actual vocabulary. Decide if the word/phrase is used correctly according to its meaning as established in the text.
statements: "The mechanism was described as self-correcting, requiring constant deliberate government intervention to function."
"Analysts describe Britain's 1925 return to gold as vindicated by subsequent economic difficulties."
"The gold discoveries eased what might otherwise have been a persistently deflationary bias in the system."
"The interwar arrangement was considerably more fragile than its prewar predecessor, collapsing rapidly under stress."
"The pound's decline was confined to a single trading session, lasting only a few hours in total."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "The mechanism was described as self-correcting, requiring constant deliberate government intervention to function."**

In paragraph (2), the self-correcting price-specie flow restores balance "without any deliberate policy intervention." Pairing "self-correcting" with "constant deliberate government intervention" contradicts the passage sense of the term.

**Trap:** Self-correcting sounds technical enough to hide an antonym paraphrase.

Self-correcting means no deliberate intervention, so the sentence's meaning is **false** against the text.

**B) "Analysts describe Britain's 1925 return to gold as vindicated by subsequent economic difficulties."**

Paragraph (5) says many historians regard Keynes's prediction as "substantially vindicated" by Britain's subdued growth and elevated unemployment after the overvalued 1925 return. Here "vindicated" keeps that confirmed-by-later-outcomes sense tied to those difficulties.

**Tip:** Vindicated = later evidence bore the claim out — not "justified as wise policy."

The passage-backed use of vindicated fits, so the wording is **true**.

**C) "The gold discoveries eased what might otherwise have been a persistently deflationary bias in the system."**

Paragraph (3) says the Witwatersrand-driven production surge was "easing what might otherwise have been a persistently deflationary bias in a system reliant on a fixed physical commodity." The sentence restates that easing role with the same collocates.

The eased / persistently deflationary bias wording matches the passage, so the claim is **true**.

**D) "The interwar arrangement was considerably more fragile than its prewar predecessor, collapsing rapidly under stress."**

Paragraph (6) opens by saying the interwar gold exchange standard "proved considerably more fragile than its prewar predecessor," and later paragraphs show that fragility under 1930s stress. "Considerably more fragile" is the passage's own comparison.

The fragility contrast is passage-true, so the statement is **true**.

**E) "The pound's decline was confined to a single trading session, lasting only a few hours in total."**

Paragraph (7) places the ~25% fall "within a matter of months," not inside one session of a few hours. The sentence invents an ultra-short collapse the text never describes.

**Trap:** Months → hours shrinks the timeline without any supporting span.

The passage times the decline in months, so the few-hours version is **false**.
highlights: restoring balance without any deliberate policy intervention
a prediction many economic historians now regard as substantially vindicated by Britain's subdued growth and elevated unemployment
easing what might otherwise have been a persistently deflationary bias
The interwar gold exchange standard proved considerably more fragile than its prewar predecessor
the pound's value fell by approximately 25% against gold-backed currencies within a matter of months

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly written, using a word or phrase echoing the passage. Decide if the word/ phrase is used correctly according to its meaning as established in the text.
statements: "The devaluation was an explicit effort to raise domestic price levels and combat deflationary pressures."
"The system's golden age depended heavily on cooperative arrangements beyond the automatic mechanism alone."
"A cascading crisis of convertibility means that confidence problems remained isolated to a single country."
"The layering of reserve promises across multiple currencies increased, rather than reduced, systemic vulnerability."
"Britain's wartime spending is described as having stayed roughly level with pre-war annual expenditure."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "The devaluation was an explicit effort to raise domestic price levels and combat deflationary pressures."**

Paragraph (7) describes Roosevelt's gold move as made "in an explicit effort to raise domestic price levels and combat the deflationary pressures of the Great Depression." The sentence's purpose language tracks that phrasing.

The raise-prices / fight-deflation purpose matches the passage, so the wording is **true**.

**B) "The system's golden age depended heavily on cooperative arrangements beyond the automatic mechanism alone."**

Paragraph (3) stresses that golden-age stability "depended heavily on factors beyond the automatic mechanism itself," including London's role and cooperative following of the Bank of England's discount rate. Paragraph (8) later names the "informal cooperative arrangements" that had sustained the system before 1914.

Cooperation beyond the automatic model is exactly the passage's caveat, so the claim is **true**.

**C) "A cascading crisis of convertibility means that confidence problems remained isolated to a single country."**

Paragraph (6) says a loss of confidence in sterling or the dollar could "trigger a cascading crisis of convertibility across many countries simultaneously." Cascading means spread, not isolation — the sentence invents the opposite definition.

**Trap:** Cascading sounds dramatic but always implies multi-link spillover, not containment.

Cascading crisis = multi-country spillover, so "isolated to a single country" is **false**.

**D) "The layering of reserve promises across multiple currencies increased, rather than reduced, systemic vulnerability."**

Paragraph (6) explains that holding gold plus foreign currencies as reserves meant confidence loss could cascade across many countries — "a vulnerability the classical system had not shared to nearly the same degree." Layering promises raised exposure; it did not dampen it.

The passage treats multi-currency layering as more vulnerable, so the statement is **true**.

**E) "Britain's wartime spending is described as having stayed roughly level with pre-war annual expenditure."**

Paragraph (4) says wartime spending rose to "roughly ten times" pre-war annual government expenditure by 1918. "Roughly level" erases that massive multiple.

**Trap:** Roughly softens the scale but cannot flip tenfold growth into flat spending.

The text says ~10×, not level, so the claim is **false**.
highlights: in an explicit effort to raise domestic price levels and combat the deflationary pressures of the Great Depression
depended heavily on factors beyond the automatic mechanism itself
trigger a cascading crisis of convertibility across many countries simultaneously
This layering of promises meant that a loss of confidence in sterling or the dollar could, in principle, trigger a cascading crisis
rose to a figure estimated at roughly ten times its pre-war annual government expenditure by 1918

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The just-in-time inventory model is described as having been newly invented in response to the pandemic's disruptions.
The pandemic is described as having exposed, rather than created, a vulnerability that had already been building for decades.
The 2023 survey found that 62% of executives reported reshoring/nearshoring activity, up from a 24% baseline reported in a comparable 2019 survey.
Mexico's appeal as a nearshoring destination is attributed in the passage to matching US wage levels rather than to geographic proximity and cost savings.
The passage attributes the entire FDI increase into Mexico solely to reduced exposure to transpacific shipping disruptions, excluding any other named cause.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The just-in-time inventory model is described as having been newly invented in response to the pandemic's disruptions.**

Paragraph 1 places just-in-time models in the past tense of long-standing practice: firms "had organised" supply chains around single-source suppliers using those models "for decades." The pandemic is the shock that made the existing model fail, not the moment inventing it.

**Trap:** A crisis that reveals a practice can feel like it created the practice — chronology here runs the other way.

The claim invents a post-pandemic origin the text never gives, so it fails against the decades-old framing.

**B) The pandemic is described as having exposed, rather than created, a vulnerability that had already been building for decades.**

The opening sentence of Paragraph 1 says the pandemic "exposed a structural vulnerability that had been building quietly for decades." "Exposed" is the key verb: the weakness pre-existed; COVID made it visible.

That wording matches the claim exactly, so the statement tracks the passage.

**C) The 2023 survey found that 62% of executives reported reshoring/nearshoring activity, up from a 24% baseline reported in a comparable 2019 survey.**

Paragraph 2 pairs the figures and years without mixing them: 62% in the 2023 survey versus 24% in a comparable 2019 survey, for reshoring or nearshoring at least part of production.

**Tip:** Keep the year stuck to its percentage — swapping 62% onto 2019 is a common trap.

Both percentages and both years line up with the text, so the claim holds.

**D) Mexico's appeal as a nearshoring destination is attributed in the passage to matching US wage levels rather than to geographic proximity and cost savings.**

Paragraph 3 credits Mexico with "geographic proximity without the full cost of domestic production," and ties FDI growth to lower transport costs and less transpacific disruption exposure. Wage parity with the US is never offered as the reason.

The statement swaps in an invented wage-match motive, so it fails.

**E) The passage attributes the entire FDI increase into Mexico solely to reduced exposure to transpacific shipping disruptions, excluding any other named cause.**

Paragraph 3 says the rise was "driven partly by lower transportation costs and reduced exposure to transpacific shipping disruptions." Two causes are named, and "partly" already blocks an exclusive single-cause reading.

**Trap:** "Solely" / "entirely" items collapse a two-factor list into one.

The exclusivity claim contradicts the dual driver in the text, so the statement is false.
highlights: had organised their supply chains around globally dispersed, single-source suppliers operating under justin-time inventory models
exposed a structural vulnerability that had been building quietly for decades
62% reported having reshored or nearshored at least part of their production within the previous three years, a sharp rise from just 24%
seeking geographic proximity without the full cost of domestic production
driven partly by lower transportation costs and reduced exposure to transpacific shipping disruptions

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The narrowing US-China labour cost ratio is attributed to a combination of rising Chinese wages and increased automation, not to automation alone.
The labour cost ratio narrowed from roughly 8:1 in 2010 to about 4:1 by 2023, a reduction of half the original gap.
A firm publicly announcing reshoring plans is treated in the passage as functionally equivalent to a firm that has already completed that shift.
The typical delay firms experienced beyond their original reshoring timeline is attributed mainly to falling demand for their products.
The passage treats "friend-shoring" as a more precise label for what is often loosely called "reshoring," rather than as an identical process.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The narrowing US-China labour cost ratio is attributed to a combination of rising Chinese wages and increased automation, not to automation alone.**

Paragraph 4 names both drivers in one phrase: the ratio fell "driven by rising wages in China and by increased automation." Automation is necessary but not sole.

The joint attribution matches the claim, so the statement is true.

**B) The labour cost ratio narrowed from roughly 8:1 in 2010 to about 4:1 by 2023, a reduction of half the original gap.**

The same paragraph gives "roughly 8:1 in 2010" and "about 4:1 by 2023." Halving an 8:1 gap yields 4:1, so the arithmetic paraphrase is faithful.

The figures and the half-gap reading both fit the passage, so the claim stands.

**C) A firm publicly announcing reshoring plans is treated in the passage as functionally equivalent to a firm that has already completed that shift.**

Paragraph 5 separates announcement from completion: of companies that "publicly announced reshoring plans," "only 15% had actually completed the announced shift" on the original timeline. Announcement and completion are precisely not treated as the same.

**Trap:** Public intent language often masquerades as done facts in exam items.

The equivalence claim erases that gap, so it fails.

**D) The typical delay firms experienced beyond their original reshoring timeline is attributed mainly to falling demand for their products.**

Delays are pinned to "permitting delays, skilled-labour shortages, and unexpected construction costs." Falling demand never appears.

The statement invents a demand cause the text does not name, so it is false.

**E) The passage treats "friend-shoring" as a more precise label for what is often loosely called "reshoring," rather than as an identical process.**

Paragraph 6 says much of what is "publicly labelled 'reshoring'" "more accurately reflects" moves to allied or trusted third countries, "sometimes termed 'friend-shoring.'" The passage corrects the label; it does not collapse the two into one process.

That precision frame matches the claim, so the statement holds.
highlights: driven by rising wages in China and by increased automation
fell from roughly 8:1 in 2010 to about 4:1 by 2023
only 15% had actually completed the announced shift within their originally stated timeframe
often due to permitting delays, skilled-labour shortages, and unexpected construction costs
publicly labelled "reshoring" more accurately reflects diversification toward allied or trusted third countries, a practice sometimes termed "friend-shoring,"

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The EU's Chips Act is described as targeting a doubling of the EU's own global semiconductor production share, not an absolute doubling of total global output.
The EU's Chips Act aims to raise the EU's share of global semiconductor production from approximately 20% to 40% by 2030.
Higher domestic labour and compliance costs are cited as the reason reshored production costs more per unit than its offshored equivalent.
The gap between reshored and offshored production costs is described as being absorbed primarily through higher consumer prices.
The continued growth of manufacturing hubs like Vietnam and India is presented as evidence against a simple, one-directional reversal of globalisation.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The EU's Chips Act is described as targeting a doubling of the EU's own global semiconductor production share, not an absolute doubling of total global output.**

Paragraph 7 aims at "doubling the EU's share of global semiconductor production" — a relative slice of the world total, not a doubling of all chips made worldwide.

Share versus absolute output is the distinction the claim gets right, so it matches the text.

**B) The EU's Chips Act aims to raise the EU's share of global semiconductor production from approximately 20% to 40% by 2030.**

The passage doubles "from approximately 10% to 20% by 2030." The statement doubles the wrong baseline (20%→40%).

**Trap:** Same "doubling" story, swapped percentages.

The wrong start and end percentages overturn the claim.

**C) Higher domestic labour and compliance costs are cited as the reason reshored production costs more per unit than its offshored equivalent.**

Paragraph 8 estimates reshored units cost 20–25% more, "reflecting higher domestic labour and compliance costs." That is exactly the reason named.

The cost drivers line up with the statement, so it is true.

**D) The gap between reshored and offshored production costs is described as being absorbed primarily through higher consumer prices.**

Only "roughly 3% to 5%" of the gap is passed to consumers; "the remainder" is absorbed via thinner margins or automation gains — so consumers are explicitly not the main sponge.

The "primarily through higher consumer prices" reading reverses the text, so the claim fails.

**E) The continued growth of manufacturing hubs like Vietnam and India is presented as evidence against a simple, one-directional reversal of globalisation.**

Paragraph 9 says those hubs' rise suggests networks "may be being rerouted and diversified rather than straightforwardly reversed." Growth elsewhere is offered as a counter to a clean reverse-globalisation story.

That use of the hubs matches the claim, so the statement stands.
highlights: doubling the EU's share of global semiconductor production from approximately 10% to 20% by 2030
from approximately 10% to 20% by 2030
reflecting higher domestic labour and compliance costs
only a modest fraction of this gap, roughly 3% to 5%, is ultimately passed on to consumers
may be being rerouted and diversified rather than straightforwardly reversed

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Statements test whether a plausible-sounding inference is actually supported by the passage, ordered by the paragraph each relies on, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Since automation is named as one factor narrowing the labour cost ratio, it can be concluded that automation alone fully explains the shift.
The labour cost ratio's narrowing from 8:1 to 4:1 is, by simple arithmetic, a reduction of exactly half the original gap.
A firm reporting it has "reshored part of its production" is not automatically the same, by the passage's own logic, as a firm that has completed a full transition.
Because nearshoring benefited Mexico, the passage implies Mexican labour costs converged with those in the United States.
Since reshored production costs more per unit, the passage implies that reduced profit margins are the only way firms can absorb that extra cost.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Since automation is named as one factor narrowing the labour cost ratio, it can be concluded that automation alone fully explains the shift.**

Paragraph 4 lists automation beside rising Chinese wages. Naming "one factor" never licences wiping out the other.

**Trap:** "Since X is mentioned…" leaps to "X is the whole cause."

The sole-cause leap overreaches the joint drivers, so the inference fails.

**B) The labour cost ratio's narrowing from 8:1 to 4:1 is, by simple arithmetic, a reduction of exactly half the original gap.**

The stated path from "roughly 8:1" to "about 4:1" is arithmetically a halving of the original gap; the claim stays inside that inference.

The arithmetic follows the passage figures, so the statement is true.

**C) A firm reporting it has "reshored part of its production" is not automatically the same, by the passage's own logic, as a firm that has completed a full transition.**

Survey language of reshoring "at least part" of production (Paragraph 2) and the sharp drop from announced plans to completed shifts (Paragraph 5) both warn against equating partial or announced moves with a finished full transition.

The caution matches the claim, so it holds.

**D) Because nearshoring benefited Mexico, the passage implies Mexican labour costs converged with those in the United States.**

Mexico's benefit is tied to proximity and cost savings versus full US domestic production — not to Mexican wages meeting US wages. Wage-ratio language elsewhere concerns US–China, not Mexico–US.

The wage-convergence implication is unsupported, so the statement fails.

**E) Since reshored production costs more per unit, the passage implies that reduced profit margins are the only way firms can absorb that extra cost.**

Paragraph 8 lists remaining absorption via "reduced profit margins or offset by automation-driven productivity gains" — two paths, not one exclusive door.

**Trap:** "Only way" collapses an or-list.

The exclusivity twist contradicts the dual offset, so the inference is false.
highlights: driven by rising wages in China and by increased automation
fell from roughly 8:1 in 2010 to about 4:1 by 2023
only 15% had actually completed the announced shift within their originally stated timeframe
seeking geographic proximity without the full cost of domestic production
absorbed through reduced profit margins or offset by automation-driven productivity gains

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Statements require linking details across the passage in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The gap between high reported reshoring intentions and low actual completion rates suggests some firms discuss reshoring more readily than they execute it.
The average delay of roughly 18 months beyond original targets is consistent with the passage's broader caution against taking announced reshoring intentions at face value.

Because friend-shoring is distinguished from genuine reshoring, and because Vietnam's import share grew, it follows that Vietnam itself has become a genuine reshoring destination for US manufacturers.
The narrowing labour cost ratio helps explain why reshoring has become more feasible, even though the passage still treats reshored production as costlier overall.
Because the passage raises genuine uncertainty about whether this shift is durable, it can be concluded that the statistical trends presented earlier must therefore be considered unreliable.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The gap between high reported reshoring intentions and low actual completion rates suggests some firms discuss reshoring more readily than they execute it.**

Paragraph 5 cautions against taking announced intentions "at face value" and shows only 15% finishing on the stated timeline. That gap between talk and finished relocation supports reading announcements as easier than execution.

The synthesis stays inside the passage's own caution, so the claim is true.

**B) The average delay of roughly 18 months beyond original targets is consistent with the passage's broader caution against taking announced reshoring intentions at face value.**

The same paragraph pairs the face-value warning with "average delays of roughly 18 months beyond their initial targets." The delay is concrete evidence for that caution, not a rival story.

The numeric detail reinforces the warning, so the statement holds.

**C) Because friend-shoring is distinguished from genuine reshoring, and because Vietnam's import share grew, it follows that Vietnam itself has become a genuine reshoring destination for US manufacturers.**

Vietnam's rising share illustrates "a rerouting… away from China rather than a repatriation of manufacturing to the United States itself." Friend-shoring is third-country diversification; calling Vietnam "genuine reshoring" flips that distinction.

**Trap:** Rising third-country hubs ≠ home-country return.

The conclusion mislabels Vietnam as reshoring, so it fails.

**D) The narrowing labour cost ratio helps explain why reshoring has become more feasible, even though the passage still treats reshored production as costlier overall.**

Paragraph 4 presents the narrowed ratio as making the shift "more feasible," while Paragraph 8 still prices reshored units 20–25% above the offshored equivalent. Feasible-er and still costlier can both be true.

The two claims coexist in the text, so the synthesis stands.

**E) Because the passage raises genuine uncertainty about whether this shift is durable, it can be concluded that the statistical trends presented earlier must therefore be considered unreliable.**

Paragraph 9 debates durability — structural reversal versus temporary shock — without questioning whether the earlier survey percentages or FDI figures are accurate. Uncertain future is not the same as unreliable past data.

The leap from debate-about-future to "statistics are unreliable" invents a charge the text never makes, so the claim fails.
highlights: critics caution against taking announced reshoring intentions at face value
average delays of roughly 18 months beyond their initial targets
rather than a repatriation of manufacturing to the United States itself
cost between 20% and 25% more per unit than the offshored equivalent
remains a matter of active debate among economists

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.exam_title: Grammar Rules (New Sentences, Anchored in Text Vocabulary)
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "Had firms not diversified their supplier base earlier, the disruption would have proven even more severe."
"The board recommended that the company reassesses its exposure to single-source suppliers."
"The number of manufacturers reconsidering their sourcing strategy continue to grow."
"Neither the subsidy nor the tax credits were enough to fully offset the higher labour costs."
"Having relocated part of its production, the firm reduced its exposure to shipping disruptions."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Had firms not diversified their supplier base earlier, the disruption would have proven even more severe."**

This is a well-formed third conditional with inverted protasis: "Had firms not diversified…" stands for "If firms had not diversified…," and the main clause correctly uses "would have proven." No auxiliary is missing, and the time sequence (earlier diversification → past disruption counterfactual) is coherent.

The inverted conditional is formed correctly, so the sentence is sound.

**B) "The board recommended that the company reassesses its exposure to single-source suppliers."**

After "recommended that," English prefers the subjunctive (or mandative) base form: "reassess," not indicative "reassesses." The plural-looking third-person -s marks the wrong mood.

**Trap:** Normal present-tense agreement after recommend/suggest + that.

Repair to "…that the company reassess…," so the line as written fails.

**C) "The number of manufacturers reconsidering their sourcing strategy continue to grow."**

The grammatical subject is singular "The number," so the verb must be "continues," not plural "continue." What follows "of" does not control agreement.

Subject–verb agreement collapses here; the sound version is "…continues to grow," so the sentence fails.

**D) "Neither the subsidy nor the tax credits were enough to fully offset the higher labour costs."**

With "neither…nor," the verb commonly agrees with the nearer noun. Here "tax credits" is plural, so "were" is the expected choice.

Proximity agreement is applied correctly, so the wording stands.

**E) "Having relocated part of its production, the firm reduced its exposure to shipping disruptions."**

The participial opener "Having relocated…" attaches to "the firm," which is logically the relocator — no dangling modifier. Perfect participle plus past main clause is a clean sequence.

The participle and subject line up, so the sentence is true.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "No sooner had the factory reopened than orders began to resume."
"The subsidy, along with several tax incentives, were introduced to accelerate the transition."
"Each of the surveyed manufacturers have reported some disruption to their supply chain."
"By the time the program concludes, several new facilities will have already opened."
"The data, which were gathered across multiple sectors, point to a broadly consistent pattern."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "No sooner had the factory reopened than orders began to resume."**

"No sooner…than" correctly triggers inversion ("had the factory reopened") and pairs past perfect with a following simple past ("began"). The correlative "than" (not "when") is the right partner.

The correlative inversion pattern is intact, so the sentence holds.

**B) "The subsidy, along with several tax incentives, were introduced to accelerate the transition."**

"Along with several tax incentives" is a parenthetical add-on; the head subject remains singular "The subsidy," which needs "was introduced," not "were."

**Trap:** The nearest plural noun after the comma steals agreement.

Repair to "…was introduced…," so the written verb fails.

**C) "Each of the surveyed manufacturers have reported some disruption to their supply chain."**

"Each of" takes a singular verb even when a plural noun follows: "has reported," not "have reported."

Agreement is wrong for "each"; the sentence does not stand.

**D) "By the time the program concludes, several new facilities will have already opened."**

"By the time" plus a future reference point calls for future perfect to mark completion before that point: "will have…opened" is the right shape, with "already" naturally sitting inside it.

The future-perfect framing fits the deadline, so the wording is true.

**E) "The data, which were gathered across multiple sectors, point to a broadly consistent pattern."**

Here "data" is treated as plural throughout: "were gathered" and plural "point" agree with that choice. The relative clause and main verb stay consistent.

Plural treatment of "data" is applied cleanly, so the sentence stands.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "Despite of the higher costs involved, several firms proceeded with relocation plans."
"Whoever oversees the transition should account for delays typically involved in construction."
"The firm denied having deliberately overstated its reshoring progress."
"There is several reasons why completion rates remained so low."
"The initiative, which was funded over several years, aims to expand domestic capacity."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Despite of the higher costs involved, several firms proceeded with relocation plans."**

"Despite" never takes "of"; the paired idiom is "in spite of." Written "Despite of" is a fusion error.

**Trap:** Cross-contamination from "in spite of."

Repair to "Despite the higher costs…" or "In spite of the higher costs…," so the line fails.

**B) "Whoever oversees the transition should account for delays typically involved in construction."**

"Whoever" correctly heads the subject clause; "oversees" agrees with that indefinite singular subject, and "should account" is a natural predicate for the whole clause.

The free-relative subject is formed properly, so the sentence is sound.

**C) "The firm denied having deliberately overstated its reshoring progress."**

After "denied," the perfect gerund "having…overstated" correctly marks a prior alleged act. Adverb placement ("deliberately") inside the gerund is natural.

The verb pattern matches the meaning, so the wording holds.

**D) "There is several reasons why completion rates remained so low."**

Existential "there" agreement tracks the notional noun: plural "reasons" needs "There are," not "There is."

**Trap:** Habitual "there's" in speech before plural nouns.

Repair to "There are several reasons…," so the sentence fails.

**E) "The initiative, which was funded over several years, aims to expand domestic capacity."**

Singular "initiative" takes singular verbs in both the relative clause ("was funded") and the main clause ("aims"). The non-restrictive clause is well attached.

Agreement stays consistent, so the sentence is true.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly written, using a word or phrase echoing the passage's vocabulary. Decide if the word/phrase is used correctly according to its established meaning.
statements: "The strategy aimed to strengthen resilience by concentrating production in a single overseas facility."
"The narrowing cost gap made relocation more economically viable for several manufacturers."
"Government funding was allocated to expand domestic production capacity in strategic sectors."
"The firm's diversification strategy left it wholly dependent on a single foreign supplier."
"Automation helped offset rising domestic costs by improving overall productivity."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "The strategy aimed to strengthen resilience by concentrating production in a single overseas facility."**

In this bank's supply-chain sense, resilience is built by reducing single-source exposure, not by concentrating everything in one overseas plant. The sentence uses "resilience" with the opposite strategy.

**Trap:** Putting all eggs in one "efficient" basket looks decisive but is the vulnerability the passage describes.

The collocation reverses the established meaning, so the wording fails.

**B) "The narrowing cost gap made relocation more economically viable for several manufacturers."**

"Narrowing cost gap" plus "more economically viable" tracks the passage logic that a smaller labour-cost differential makes relocation more feasible. The adjectives and nouns match ordinary usage.

The meaning lines up with the established sense, so the sentence stands.

**C) "Government funding was allocated to expand domestic production capacity in strategic sectors."**

"Allocated…to expand…capacity" is the same natural funding collocation used for the CHIPS / Chips Acts. Nothing is twisted.

The wording matches standard use, so it is true.

**D) "The firm's diversification strategy left it wholly dependent on a single foreign supplier."**

Diversification means spreading exposure across sources; "wholly dependent on a single foreign supplier" is concentration, the opposite outcome. The sentence forces contradictory poles into one strategy label.

That clash of meanings overturns the claim.

**E) "Automation helped offset rising domestic costs by improving overall productivity."**

"Offset…by improving…productivity" is a standard collocation and matches how the passage describes automation absorbing part of the reshoring cost gap.

The usage is natural and text-aligned, so the sentence holds.
highlights: single-source suppliers operating under justin-time inventory models that minimised stockpiles in favour of efficiency
this shift has been made more feasible by a narrowing cost differential
allocated $52 billion in subsidies to expand domestic semiconductor manufacturing capacity
diversification toward allied or trusted third countries
offset by automation-driven productivity gains

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly written, using a word or phrase echoing the passage. Decide if the word/ phrase is used correctly according to its established meaning.
statements: "Friend-shoring refers to relocating production entirely back to one's own home country."
"The company's exposure to single-source risk was reduced after diversifying its supplier base."
"The subsidy was described as sufficient to fully eliminate the cost gap between relocated and offshored production."
"Reshored production is generally described in the passage as costlier per unit than its offshored equivalent."
"The trend's long-term durability is treated in the passage as a matter of active, unresolved debate."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Friend-shoring refers to relocating production entirely back to one's own home country."**

In the passage, friend-shoring is diversification toward allied or trusted third countries, expressly contrasted with a "genuine return of production to the home country." Home-country return is reshoring proper, not friend-shoring.

**Trap:** Any "-shoring" word can be misread as "bring it all home."

The definition swaps friend-shoring for genuine reshoring, so the claim fails.

**B) "The company's exposure to single-source risk was reduced after diversifying its supplier base."**

Diversifying the supplier base and reducing single-source exposure are the paired meaning the passage builds from Paragraph 1's vulnerability. The causal link is ordinary and correct.

The wording matches established usage, so the sentence is true.

**C) "The subsidy was described as sufficient to fully eliminate the cost gap between relocated and offshored production."**

The text never says subsidies wipe out the gap; reshored production still costs "20% and 25% more per unit," with only a modest consumer share and margins/automation covering the rest. "Fully eliminate" invents a claim.

That absolute wipeout overstates what subsidies do in the passage, so the statement fails.

**D) "Reshored production is generally described in the passage as costlier per unit than its offshored equivalent."**

Paragraph 8 states reshored production costs "between 20% and 25% more per unit than the offshored equivalent." "Costlier per unit" is a faithful paraphrase.

The cost comparison matches the text, so the claim holds.

**E) "The trend's long-term durability is treated in the passage as a matter of active, unresolved debate."**

The close of Paragraph 9 says whether the reordering is durable or temporary "remains a matter of active debate among economists." "Unresolved debate" tracks that framing.

The sentence mirrors the passage conclusion, so it stands.
highlights: diversification toward allied or trusted third countries, a practice sometimes termed "friend-shoring,"
globally dispersed, single-source suppliers
cost between 20% and 25% more per unit than the offshored equivalent
cost between 20% and 25% more per unit than the offshored equivalent
remains a matter of active debate among economists

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The severe economic distress described in Paragraph 1 is attributed partly to a chronic shortage of US dollars needed to purchase fuel, machinery, and raw materials.
Marshall's proposal, as described in Paragraph 2, required European governments to coordinate their reconstruction efforts jointly rather than negotiate purely bilateral aid requests.
Czechoslovakia is described as having withdrawn from the programme entirely on its own initiative, without any external pressure being involved.
The programme's total disbursement of approximately $13.3 billion was distributed over a four-year period following Congressional authorisation in April 1948.
The United Kingdom is described as having received a smaller share of total aid than France.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The severe economic distress described in Paragraph 1 is attributed partly to a chronic shortage of US dollars needed to purchase fuel, machinery, and raw materials.**

Paragraph 1 lists several causes of Europe's post-war distress, and one of them is explicit: a chronic US-dollar shortage left governments unable to buy fuel, machinery, and raw materials for rebuilding. The statement restates that causal link without adding outside claims.

**Tip:** When a statement names a cause plus the imports blocked by it, check that both pieces sit in the same paragraph stretch.

That dollar-shortage wording matches Paragraph 1, so the claim lines up with the passage.

**B) Marshall's proposal, as described in Paragraph 2, required European governments to coordinate their reconstruction efforts jointly rather than negotiate purely bilateral aid requests.**

Paragraph 2 presents Marshall's Harvard proposal as conditional on joint European coordination of reconstruction, rather than each country seeking purely bilateral aid. That is exactly the contrast the statement draws.

The joint-coordination condition in Paragraph 2 supports the claim as written.

**C) Czechoslovakia is described as having withdrawn from the programme entirely on its own initiative, without any external pressure being involved.**

Paragraph 2 says Czechoslovakia initially showed interest, then "was compelled by Soviet pressure to withdraw." The exit is coerced, not a free solo decision. The statement invents "own initiative" and erases the Soviet pressure the text names.

**Trap:** Initial interest can look like voluntary exit if you stop reading before the compulsion clause.

Because withdrawal is forced by Soviet pressure, the "own initiative" claim fails against the passage.

**D) The programme's total disbursement of approximately $13.3 billion was distributed over a four-year period following Congressional authorisation in April 1948.**

Paragraph 3 places Congressional authorisation in April 1948 via the Economic Cooperation Act, then states that over the following four years the programme paid out about $13.3 billion. Timing and total both match the statement.

The four-year, $13.3 billion sequence after April 1948 is what Paragraph 3 reports, so the claim holds.

**E) The United Kingdom is described as having received a smaller share of total aid than France.**

Paragraph 3 ranks recipients: the United Kingdom took the largest share at roughly 24%, with France next at about 20%. The statement reverses that order and treats the UK as the smaller recipient.

**Trap:** Later Austria/UK national-income percentages (Paragraph 8) are relative weight, not the same ranking as absolute shares of the aid pot.

Because the UK outranks France at 24% versus 20%, the smaller-share claim does not match the passage.
highlights: a chronic shortage of US dollars left European governments unable to purchase the fuel, machinery, and raw materials needed to rebuild
conditional on European governments jointly coordinating their own reconstruction efforts rather than each simply requesting bilateral assistance
was compelled by Soviet pressure to withdraw its participation within weeks
Over the following four years, the programme disbursed a total of approximately $13.3 billion in grants and loans
with the United Kingdom receiving the largest single share at roughly 24% of the total, followed by France at approximately 20%

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The plan's conditions are described as extending beyond fund transfers to include tariff reduction and currency stabilisation requirements.
Institutional cooperation fostered by the OEEC is presented as having laid groundwork for later European economic integration.
The programme's containment rationale is described as being always publicly acknowledged by American officials at the time.
Communist parties in France and Italy are described in the passage as having drawn political strength partly from post-war economic hardship.
Milward argued that Western European industrial output had already reached roughly 111% of its 1938 level by the time large-scale disbursements began in 1948.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The plan's conditions are described as extending beyond fund transfers to include tariff reduction and currency stabilisation requirements.**

Paragraph 4 opens by saying the plan's conditions went well beyond money transfers. Recipients had to cut tariffs and trade barriers, stabilise currencies, and accept mutual oversight through the OEEC. Tariff cuts and currency stabilisation are named conditions, not optional extras.

Those beyond-funds requirements in Paragraph 4 make the statement a faithful paraphrase.

**B) Institutional cooperation fostered by the OEEC is presented as having laid groundwork for later European economic integration.**

Paragraph 4 reports that many historians see the OEEC-centred cooperation as laying essential groundwork for deeper European economic integration, which later produced the European Economic Community. "Groundwork" is the passage's own word for that contribution.

The groundwork-for-integration reading matches Paragraph 4, so the claim stands.

**C) The programme's containment rationale is described as being always publicly acknowledged by American officials at the time.**

Paragraph 5 says architects framed the programme as Cold War containment "explicitly, if not always publicly." That qualifier means public acknowledgment was not constant. "Always publicly acknowledged" flips the hedge into its opposite.

**Trap:** "Explicitly" describes how they framed the tool, not how openly they advertised it every time.

Because the text says "if not always publicly," the always-public claim fails.

**D) Communist parties in France and Italy are described in the passage as having drawn political strength partly from post-war economic hardship.**

Paragraph 5 links American hopes of reducing communist appeal to France, Italy, and elsewhere, and notes that post-war economic hardship had contributed to those parties' electoral strength. Hardship is a partial cause of that strength, just as the statement says.

That hardship-to-electoral-strength link in Paragraph 5 supports the claim.

**E) Milward argued that Western European industrial output had already reached roughly 111% of its 1938 level by the time large-scale disbursements began in 1948.**

Paragraph 6 attributes to Alan Milward the claim that Western European industrial output was already about 111% of its 1938 level when large-scale Marshall disbursements began flowing in 1948. Figure, baseline year, and timing all align.

Milward's 111%-of-1938 output argument in Paragraph 6 is exactly what the statement reports.
highlights: Recipient governments were required to reduce tariffs and other barriers to intra-European trade, stabilise their currencies
laid essential groundwork for the deeper European economic integration that would eventually produce the European Economic Community
framed it explicitly, if not always publicly, as a tool of Cold War containment
where post-war economic hardship had contributed to their electoral strength
Western European industrial output had already recovered to roughly 111% of its 1938 level by the time large-scale disbursements began flowing in 1948

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Milward and others attributed the recovery visible by 1948 mainly to domestic factors such as currency stabilisation and rising savings rates.
Proponents of the traditional view argued that Marshall aid played no meaningful role in relieving the dollar shortage regardless of domestic recovery momentum.
In Austria, Marshall assistance amounted to as much as 14% of national income in some years, compared to under 3% in the United Kingdom.
The passage presents a single, universally agreed conclusion about whether the Marshall Plan was the decisive driver of recovery.
The ongoing historical debate about the Marshall Plan is described as paralleling later disputes over foreign aid effectiveness in other contexts.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Milward and others attributed the recovery visible by 1948 mainly to domestic factors such as currency stabilisation and rising savings rates.**

Paragraph 7 says Milward and others pointed instead to domestic drivers—currency stabilisation, rising savings, and pent-up demand after wartime rationing—as more decisive for the recovery already visible by 1948. The statement correctly names that domestic attribution.

Those domestic-factor claims in Paragraph 7 match the statement.

**B) Proponents of the traditional view argued that Marshall aid played no meaningful role in relieving the dollar shortage regardless of domestic recovery momentum.**

Paragraph 7's traditional camp argued the opposite: Marshall aid was "nonetheless critical in relieving the dollar shortage" that would otherwise have forced import cuts, even if domestic momentum existed. "No meaningful role" erases that critical-relief claim.

**Trap:** Critics minimise aid's driving role; traditional proponents still call dollar-shortage relief critical.

Because proponents call aid critical for easing the dollar shortage, the "no meaningful role" line fails.

**C) In Austria, Marshall assistance amounted to as much as 14% of national income in some years, compared to under 3% in the United Kingdom.**

Paragraph 8 contrasts relative aid burdens: Austria reached as much as 14% of national income in some programme years, while the UK figure stayed under 3% throughout. Both percentages appear as stated.

The 14% Austria versus under-3% UK contrast is Paragraph 8's own comparison, so the claim holds.

**D) The passage presents a single, universally agreed conclusion about whether the Marshall Plan was the decisive driver of recovery.**

Paragraph 9 leaves the decisive-engine versus secondary-contribution question as "a matter of ongoing historical debate," not a settled consensus. "Single, universally agreed conclusion" invents closure the text refuses.

**Trap:** Strong closing sentences still can announce unresolved debate rather than a winner.

Because Paragraph 9 frames the issue as ongoing debate, the universal-conclusion claim does not match the passage.

**E) The ongoing historical debate about the Marshall Plan is described as paralleling later disputes over foreign aid effectiveness in other contexts.**

Paragraph 9 says the Marshall Plan debate "closely parallels later disputes over the effectiveness of foreign aid in other contexts and eras." The parallel is explicit, not inferred.

That parallel to later foreign-aid disputes matches Paragraph 9, so the statement stands.
highlights: currency stabilisation measures, rising savings rates, and pent-up consumer demand following years of wartime rationing, as more decisive drivers of the recovery already visible by 1948
Marshall aid was nonetheless critical in relieving the dollar shortage

as much as 14% of national income in some years of the programme, reflecting the country's particularly acute post-war needs, whereas in the United Kingdom, a considerably larger economy, the equivalent figure remained under 3%
remains a matter of ongoing historical debate
closely parallels later disputes over the effectiveness of foreign aid in other contexts and eras

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Statements test whether a plausible-sounding inference is actually supported by the passage, ordered by the paragraph each relies on, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Since the OEEC was formed to administer aid collectively, it can be inferred that each participating country had equal decision-making weight regardless of its size or need.
Because the plan's conditions included trade liberalisation, the passage implies economic cooperation was valued as an end in itself, not merely as a condition for receiving aid.
If the total aid of $13.3 billion was distributed evenly across all 16 participating countries, each would have received approximately $831 million.
Because Milward cited a 111%-of-1938 output figure, the passage implies he believed the Marshall Plan had no effect whatsoever on European recovery.
Because Austria's aid represented a much higher share of its national income than the UK's, it can be inferred that Austria received a larger absolute dollar amount of aid than the UK.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Since the OEEC was formed to administer aid collectively, it can be inferred that each participating country had equal decision-making weight regardless of its size or need.**

Collective administration does not imply equal votes. Paragraph 3 says remaining shares were divided "according to need and negotiated allocation formulas," which already signals unequal treatment. Equal decision-making weight is an extra leap the text never authorises.

**Trap:** "Collectively" describes joint administration, not one-country-one-vote power.

Need-based negotiated shares contradict equal weight, so the inference fails.

**B) Because the plan's conditions included trade liberalisation, the passage implies economic cooperation was valued as an end in itself, not merely as a condition for receiving aid.**

Paragraph 4 lists tariff cuts and related reforms as requirements recipient governments had to meet to take the aid. That frames cooperation as an attached condition of the aid relationship, not as a free-standing goal divorced from receiving funds. "End in itself" overreads the conditions clause.

Conditions-for-aid wording does not license an independent "end in itself" motive, so the implication fails.

**C) If the total aid of $13.3 billion was distributed evenly across all 16 participating countries, each would have received approximately $831 million.**

Paragraph 2 names sixteen Western European participants; Paragraph 3 gives a total of about $13.3 billion. Splitting that total evenly yields roughly $831 million apiece ($13,300 million ÷ 16). The statement is a correct hypothetical arithmetic check, even though the passage itself describes uneven allocation.

**Tip:** Hypothetical even-split maths can still be true while the actual distribution was unequal.

The even-split calculation from the given total and sixteen countries is arithmetically sound, so the claim holds as stated.

**D) Because Milward cited a 111%-of-1938 output figure, the passage implies he believed the Marshall Plan had no effect whatsoever on European recovery.**

Milward uses the 111% figure to argue recovery was already substantially underway before large-scale aid could have driven it—a claim about timing and relative driving force. Paragraph 9's framing of the debate likewise allows "economically secondary" significance rather than absolute zero impact. "No effect whatsoever" escalates relative-weight criticism into total denial.

**Trap:** "Already recovering before aid drove it" is not the same slogan as "aid did nothing at all."

The 111% citation questions aid as the decisive driver, not every effect, so the zero-effect implication fails.

**E) Because Austria's aid represented a much higher share of its national income than the UK's, it can be inferred that Austria received a larger absolute dollar amount of aid than the UK.**

A high share of a smaller economy's income need not mean a larger absolute cheque. Paragraph 3 already states the United Kingdom took the largest single share of total aid (~24%). Paragraph 8's 14% versus under 3% is about relative weight of aid in national income, not absolute dollars.

**Trap:** Confusing "share of national income" with "share of the aid pot" flips Austria above the UK incorrectly.

The UK's largest absolute share overturns inferring a bigger Austrian dollar total from the higher income percentage.
highlights: according to need and negotiated allocation formulas
Recipient governments were required to reduce tariffs and other barriers to intra-European trade, stabilise their currencies
disbursed a total of approximately $13.3 billion in grants and loans
suggesting that the region's recovery was substantially underway before the aid could plausibly have driven it
with the United Kingdom receiving the largest single share at roughly 24% of the total

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Statements require linking details across the passage in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The dollar shortage described in Paragraph 1 helps explain why relieving that shortage is presented in Paragraph 7 as a key argument for the plan's importance.

Because the plan's conditions fostered cooperation (Paragraph 4) and later integration is credited to this cooperation, it follows that the Marshall Plan alone caused the eventual creation of the European Economic Community.
The four-year disbursement period described in Paragraph 3 overlaps with the period in which Milward argues output had already reached 111% of its 1938 level.
Because containment motives are described as not always public (Paragraph 5), the passage implies American officials universally concealed this rationale from all European governments at all times.
The variation in aid's share of national income across countries (Paragraph 8) is consistent with the passage's earlier point that allocation followed need rather than equal division (Paragraph 3).
tactical_explanations:
**A) The dollar shortage described in Paragraph 1 helps explain why relieving that shortage is presented in Paragraph 7 as a key argument for the plan's importance.**

Paragraph 1 makes the dollar shortage a core reason Europe could not buy rebuilding imports. Paragraph 7's traditional proponents then call Marshall aid critical precisely because it relieved that shortage. Linking the early problem to the later defence of the plan is a fair cross-paragraph reading.

The shortage-to-relief bridge across Paragraphs 1 and 7 supports the synthesis.

**B) Because the plan's conditions fostered cooperation (Paragraph 4) and later integration is credited to this cooperation, it follows that the Marshall Plan alone caused the eventual creation of the European Economic Community.**

Paragraph 4 credits institutional cooperation with laying "essential groundwork" for later integration toward the EEC. Groundwork is a contributing foundation, not sole causation. "Alone caused" upgrades a supporting role into exclusive authorship the text never claims.

**Trap:** "Laid groundwork for X" is weaker than "alone caused X."

Sole-cause wording overstates Paragraph 4's groundwork claim, so the inference fails.

**C) The four-year disbursement period described in Paragraph 3 overlaps with the period in which Milward argues output had already reached 111% of its 1938 level.**

Paragraph 3 starts large-scale disbursement after April 1948 and runs about four years. Paragraph 6 places Milward's 111%-of-1938 output claim at the moment those large-scale disbursements began flowing in 1948. The timelines meet at that 1948 onset.

The shared 1948 start of large-scale aid correctly links Paragraphs 3 and 6, so the overlap claim holds.

**D) Because containment motives are described as not always public (Paragraph 5), the passage implies American officials universally concealed this rationale from all European governments at all times.**

"If not always publicly" means disclosure was uneven or incomplete, not permanent universal secrecy toward every European government. "Universally concealed… at all times" inflates a hedge into absolute concealment.

**Trap:** "Not always public" still allows some public or semi-public framing.

The absolute-concealment gloss overstates Paragraph 5's qualifier, so the implication fails.

**E) The variation in aid's share of national income across countries (Paragraph 8) is consistent with the passage's earlier point that allocation followed need rather than equal division (Paragraph 3).**

Paragraph 3 divides remaining shares by need and negotiated formulas, not equal slices. Paragraph 8's wide gap—Austria up to 14% of national income versus the UK under 3%—illustrates uneven relative weight aligned with differing need. The two paragraphs push the same uneven-allocation logic.

Need-based allocation plus the Austria/UK income-share gap fit together, so the consistency claim holds.
highlights: Marshall aid was nonetheless critical in relieving the dollar shortage
laid essential groundwork for the deeper European economic integration
by the time large-scale disbursements began flowing in 1948
if not always publicly
according to need and negotiated allocation formulas

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.exam_title: Grammar Rules (New Sentences, Anchored in Text Vocabulary)
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "Had the dollar shortage not been relieved, several governments would have restricted imports of essential goods."
"The committee recommended that each government submits an annual report on its progress."
"The number of countries participating in the programme continue to be debated by historians."
"Neither the aid nor the accompanying conditions were welcomed unanimously by every government."
"Having stabilised its currency, the government was able to attract renewed investor confidence."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Had the dollar shortage not been relieved, several governments would have restricted imports of essential goods."**

This is a third-conditional counterfactual with inversion: Had + past participle replaces If + had. The main clause keeps would have + past participle (would have restricted), which pairs correctly with that unreal past condition.

**Tip:** Inverted Had… not… still needs would have (not would alone) in the result clause.

The Had… would have pattern is well formed, so the sentence stands.

**B) "The committee recommended that each government submits an annual report on its progress."**

After recommend that, formal English expects the subjunctive base form: submit, not the present indicative submits. The plural sense of governments does not override that mandative pattern.

**Trap:** Present -s after that can look like ordinary agreement while the subjunctive wants the bare verb.

Mandative recommend that needs submit, so the line fails — "The committee recommended that each government submit an annual report on its progress."

**C) "The number of countries participating in the programme continue to be debated by historians."**

The number of + plural noun takes a singular verb because number is the grammatical head. Continue should be continues; the plural countries only modify the of-phrase.

**Trap:** Do not let the nearest plural noun steal agreement from the number.

Singular the number needs continues, so this is false — "The number of countries participating in the programme continues to be debated by historians."

**D) "Neither the aid nor the accompanying conditions were welcomed unanimously by every government."**

With neither… nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. Here conditions is plural, so were is the right match. The earlier singular aid does not control the verb once nor introduces a plural partner.

Proximity agreement with plural conditions makes were correct, so the sentence holds.

**E) "Having stabilised its currency, the government was able to attract renewed investor confidence."**

The perfect participle Having stabilised attaches to the government, which is the logical agent that stabilised the currency. Subject and -ing meaning align, so there is no dangling modifier.

The government is the right agent after Having stabilised, so the wording is sound.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "No sooner had the aid been disbursed than reconstruction efforts visibly accelerated."
"The allocation, along with several negotiated exceptions, were finalised before the programme began."
"Each of the participating governments have agreed to the oversight conditions."
"By the time the programme concluded, most participating economies will have already recovered significantly."
"The figures, which were compiled across sixteen countries, indicate considerable variation in need."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "No sooner had the aid been disbursed than reconstruction efforts visibly accelerated."**

No sooner… than correctly pairs with past-perfect inversion (had the aid been disbursed) and a simple-past follow-on clause. The correlative is than, not when, which matches the template.

No sooner had… than… is formed correctly, so the sentence stands.

**B) "The allocation, along with several negotiated exceptions, were finalised before the programme began."**

Along with… is parenthetical; the true subject remains singular allocation. The verb must be was finalised, not were. Extra plural nouns after along with do not pluralise the head.

**Trap:** Comma-wrapped along with phrases often trick agreement toward the nearer plural.

Singular allocation needs was, so the line fails — "The allocation, along with several negotiated exceptions, was finalised before the programme began."

**C) "Each of the participating governments have agreed to the oversight conditions."**

Each of takes a singular verb even when a plural noun follows. Have agreed should be has agreed; governments is only the of-phrase object.

Each of requires has agreed, so this is false — "Each of the participating governments has agreed to the oversight conditions."

**D) "By the time the programme concluded, most participating economies will have already recovered significantly."**

By the time the programme concluded fixes a past reference point, so the main event needs past perfect (had already recovered), not future perfect will have. Future perfect looks forward from now, which clashes with a finished programme.

**Trap:** By the time often invites future perfect when the time clause is past, not future.

A past conclusion point needs had already recovered, so the sentence fails — "By the time the programme concluded, most participating economies had already recovered significantly."

**E) "The figures, which were compiled across sixteen countries, indicate considerable variation in need."**

Figures is treated as plural throughout: were compiled in the relative clause and indicate in the main clause. Plural agreement is consistent and grammatical.

Plural figures with were / indicate matches cleanly, so the wording holds.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "Despite of the conditions attached, most governments accepted the aid readily."
"Whoever administers the fund should account for the differing needs of each recipient."
"The government denied having deliberately delayed its currency stabilisation measures."
"There is several reasons why historians continue to disagree about the plan's impact."
"The programme, which was authorised in 1948, aimed to accelerate European recovery."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Despite of the conditions attached, most governments accepted the aid readily."**

Despite never takes of. Either drop of (despite the conditions) or switch to in spite of. Despite of is a common blend of the two patterns.

**Trap:** In spite of needs of; despite stands alone before a noun phrase.

Despite of is ungrammatical, so the line fails — "Despite the conditions attached, most governments accepted the aid readily."

**B) "Whoever administers the fund should account for the differing needs of each recipient."**

Whoever correctly heads the subject clause (whoever administers the fund), and should account is a well-formed modal predicate for that subject. The relative sense of whoever as "the person who" fits the advising tone.

Whoever + singular verb + should account is sound, so the sentence stands.

**C) "The government denied having deliberately delayed its currency stabilisation measures."**

After deny, a perfect gerund (having + past participle) reports a prior act as the content of the denial. Having deliberately delayed places the delay before the denying, which is the intended time relation.

Denied having… is the right pattern for a prior act, so the wording holds.

**D) "There is several reasons why historians continue to disagree about the plan's impact."**

Existential there agrees with the notional subject that follows. Several reasons is plural, so the verb must be are, not is.

**Trap:** There is feels default in speech even when a plural noun is coming.

Plural reasons needs There are, so this is false — "There are several reasons why historians continue to disagree about the plan's impact."

**E) "The programme, which was authorised in 1948, aimed to accelerate European recovery."**

The non-restrictive relative which was authorised modifies singular programme, and the main verb aimed agrees with that same singular subject. Relative and main clauses stay aligned.

Singular programme with was / aimed is consistent, so the sentence is sound.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly written, using a word or phrase echoing the passage's vocabulary. Decide if the word/phrase is used correctly according to its established meaning.
statements: "The policy was framed explicitly as a tool of containment, aiming to reduce the appeal of rival ideologies."
"Pent-up demand refers to consumer spending that has already been fully satisfied over a long period."
"The dollar shortage left governments unable to purchase the imports their reconstruction required."
"The historians' dispute centres on the relative weight assigned to domestic versus external factors."
"Containment, in this context, refers to actively expanding the political influence of a rival power."
tactical_explanations:
