Paragraph 5’s gene "spread" through horizontal transfer is biological transmission between species, not literal scattering of solid objects on a surface. "Only… literal" therefore mislabels the usage.

**Trap:** "Spread" in infection biology is usually extended transmission language, not dustpan physics.

Restricting "spread" to literal object-scattering fails against the passage’s gene-transfer sense.
highlights: This agricultural use contributes substantially to the environmental spread of resistance genes
a toll exceeding that of several long-feared infectious diseases
a prolonged gap researchers have termed the "discovery void."
carry resistance genes between entirely different bacterial species, not merely within one

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The Arctic tern is described as experiencing more daylight over the course of a year than any other creature on Earth.
Conventional tracking equipment was successfully used on Arctic terns for decades before 2010, providing detailed route data.
The geolocators attached to terns in 2010 weighed less than two grams.
Tracked terns are described as typically following a single, direct route rather than a distinctive Sshaped path.
The average recorded round-trip migration distance was approximately 70,900 kilometres, with one bird logging roughly 96,000 kilometres in a single year.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The Arctic tern is described as experiencing more daylight over the course of a year than any other creature on Earth.**

Paragraph 1 ties both polar summers’ near-continuous daylight to the tern’s hemispheric chase: it “experiences more daylight over the course of a year than any other creature on Earth.” The statement simply repeats that ranking — no stretch beyond the wording.

**Tip:** Daylight / season claims in ¶1 are usually word-for-word matches; quote before you paraphrase.

The year-round daylight crown is stated outright in ¶1, so the claim matches the passage.

**B) Conventional tracking equipment was successfully used on Arctic terns for decades before 2010, providing detailed route data.**

Paragraph 2 says the opposite: for decades the route stayed estimated because the birds “are too small and light to carry conventional tracking equipment without impairing their flight.” Success arrives only in 2010 with sub-two-gram geolocators.

**Trap:** “For decades” tempts a success story; the text uses those decades for the estimation problem, not for working conventional tags.

The line flips ¶2’s size barrier into earlier conventional success, so it fails — “too small and light to carry conventional tracking equipment.”

**C) The geolocators attached to terns in 2010 weighed less than two grams.**

Paragraph 2 names the breakthrough gear exactly: “miniaturised geolocators, weighing less than two grams,” fitted to breeding birds in Greenland and Iceland. The weight claim is a straight lift from that sentence.

The less-than-two-grams figure is explicit in ¶2, so the statement tracks the text.

**D) Tracked terns are described as typically following a single, direct route rather than a distinctive Sshaped path.**

Paragraph 3 opens by rejecting a single direct line: “Rather than following a single direct route, many tracked individuals travelled in a distinctive S-shaped path.” The statement swaps that contrast and invents “typically… direct.”

**Trap:** Watch statements that keep the vocabulary (route / path) but reverse the “rather than” structure.

It contradicts ¶3’s S-shaped drift, so it fails — “a distinctive S-shaped path,” not a single direct route.

**E) The average recorded round-trip migration distance was approximately 70,900 kilometres, with one bird logging roughly 96,000 kilometres in a single year.**

Paragraph 3 reports both figures side by side: population average “approximately 70,900 kilometres,” and one long-ranging bird “roughly 96,000 kilometres in a single year.” The statement pairs them without changing either number.

Both kilometre totals sit in ¶3 as stated, so the claim matches the passage.
highlights: experiences more daylight over the course of a year than any other creature on Earth
too small and light to carry conventional tracking equipment without impairing their flight
miniaturised geolocators, weighing less than two grams
Rather than following a single direct route, many tracked individuals travelled in a distinctive S-shaped path
approximately 70,900 kilometres, though several individual birds were recorded travelling considerably further, with one especially long-ranging bird logging a round-trip of roughly 96,000 kilometres

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Over a typical thirty-year lifespan, a single tern may accumulate roughly 2.4 million kilometres of migratory flight.
This lifetime distance is described as roughly equivalent to three round trips to the Moon.
The seasonal stopover south of Greenland is described as occurring during the northbound, rather than southbound, leg of the journey.
The stopover area is described as unusually rich in plankton and small fish during that period.
The navigational mechanisms behind the terns' migration are described as fully understood and no longer subject to scientific investigation.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Over a typical thirty-year lifespan, a single tern may accumulate roughly 2.4 million kilometres of migratory flight.**

Paragraph 4 states that figure wholesale: “a typical thirty-year lifespan” plus “roughly 2.4 million kilometres of migratory flight.” Nothing in the statement alters the lifespan frame or the total.

¶4’s lifetime total is copied cleanly, so the claim matches the passage.

**B) This lifetime distance is described as roughly equivalent to three round trips to the Moon.**

The same sentence in paragraph 4 equates that mileage with “approximately three round trips to the Moon.” The statement’s “roughly equivalent” is faithful paraphrase of that comparison.

The Moon comparison is explicit in ¶4, so the wording stands.

**C) The seasonal stopover south of Greenland is described as occurring during the northbound, rather than southbound, leg of the journey.**

Paragraph 5 places the detour on “the southbound leg of the journey,” when birds pause “south of Greenland” before continuing toward Antarctic waters. Calling it northbound reverses that direction cue.

**Trap:** Northbound / southbound swaps are classic when a named geography (Greenland) sits near both seasonal frames.

It fails because ¶5 anchors the pause on the southbound leg, not northbound.

**D) The stopover area is described as unusually rich in plankton and small fish during that period.**

Paragraph 5 calls the open ocean south of Greenland “an area unusually rich in plankton and small fish during that period,” the apparent reason for replenishing fat. The statement repeats that richness claim.

The plankton-and-fish richness is stated in ¶5, so the claim matches.

**E) The navigational mechanisms behind the terns' migration are described as fully understood and no longer subject to scientific investigation.**

Paragraph 6 opens with the opposite: mechanisms “remain only partially understood,” and disentangling them in terns has “proven difficult.” Full understanding and closed investigation are invented upgrades.

**Trap:** Listing candidate methods (magnetic field, sun, landmarks) can feel like a finished theory; ¶6 still labels the picture partial.

It fails against ¶6’s “only partially understood” framing — investigation is unfinished, not closed.
highlights: a typical thirty-year lifespan, a single Arctic tern may therefore accumulate roughly 2.4 million kilometres of migratory flight
a distance equivalent to approximately three round trips to the Moon
an intriguing seasonal detour undertaken by many individuals during the southbound leg of the journey
an area unusually rich in plankton and small fish during that period
The navigational mechanisms underlying this feat remain only partially understood

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Arctic terns are described as displaying an aggressive nest-defence strategy disproportionate to their small size.
Other bird species are described as deliberately avoiding nesting near Arctic tern colonies due to the risk of attack.
Researchers have expressed concern that shifts in wind patterns or ocean productivity could disrupt one or more stages of the migration.
The passage concludes by presenting the terns' climate resilience as a fully resolved question with a clear, agreed-upon answer.
The precision of the terns' migratory strategy is presented as potentially linked to a corresponding vulnerability to disruption.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Arctic terns are described as displaying an aggressive nest-defence strategy disproportionate to their small size.**

Paragraph 7 calls the strategy “strikingly aggressive” and “entirely disproportionate to their small size,” with dive-bombing of humans, foxes, and larger birds of prey. The statement compresses that portrait without adding claims.

¶7’s disproportionate defence is on the page, so the claim matches.

**B) Other bird species are described as deliberately avoiding nesting near Arctic tern colonies due to the risk of attack.**

Paragraph 7 says neighbouring species “sometimes deliberately nest close to Arctic tern colonies specifically to benefit from this collective defensive aggression.” Avoidance is the reverse of that choice.

**Trap:** Aggression toward intruders does not mean other nesters stay away — some hitchhike on the defence.

It fails: ¶7 has species nesting close for protection, not avoiding tern colonies.

**C) Researchers have expressed concern that shifts in wind patterns or ocean productivity could disrupt one or more stages of the migration.**

Paragraph 8 records concern that climate-linked “shifts in ocean productivity or wind patterns” could “disrupt one or more stages of the migration.” The statement reorders those two factors but keeps the content.

That climate-disruption worry is explicit in ¶8, so the claim matches.

**D) The passage concludes by presenting the terns' climate resilience as a fully resolved question with a clear, agreed-upon answer.**

Paragraph 9 frames adjustment versus vulnerability as “a question actively being investigated,” not a settled verdict. “Fully resolved” and “agreed-upon answer” invent closure the ending withholds.

**Trap:** Closing paragraphs can sound conclusive when they only pose the open question more sharply.

It fails because ¶9 leaves climate resilience under active investigation, not answered.

**E) The precision of the terns' migratory strategy is presented as potentially linked to a corresponding vulnerability to disruption.**

Paragraph 9’s contrast is exact: whether they adjust quickly enough, “or whether the very precision that makes their journey so extraordinary also makes it unusually vulnerable to disruption.” Precision and vulnerability are twinned as one research question.

¶9 itself links precision to possible vulnerability, so the claim matches.
highlights: a strikingly aggressive nest-defence strategy entirely disproportionate to their small size
deliberately nest close to Arctic tern colonies specifically to benefit from this collective defensive aggression
shifts in ocean productivity or wind patterns associated with broader climate variability could disrupt one or more stages of the migration
remains a question actively being investigated by ornithologists
the very precision that makes their journey so extraordinary also makes it unusually vulnerable to disruption

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Statements test whether a plausible-sounding inference is actually supported by the passage, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Since terns experience near-continuous daylight in both polar summers, it can be inferred that they spend virtually no time in darkness across an entire year, relative to most other migratory species.

If the average round-trip distance was approximately 70,900 kilometres, and one bird travelled roughly 96,000 kilometres, that bird travelled about 25,100 kilometres further than the population average.

Because researchers cite magnetic sensitivity, solar positioning, and visual landmarks as possible navigation mechanisms, the passage implies exactly one of these three must be solely responsible, to the exclusion of the other two.

Because the S-shaped migratory path appears linked to prevailing wind patterns, it can be inferred that the birds' route may be shaped partly by energy-efficiency considerations rather than being a purely direct geographic path.

Since other species nest near tern colonies to benefit from their aggression, it can be inferred that Arctic terns' defensive behaviour can produce ecological benefits for neighbouring species, not just for the terns themselves.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Since terns experience near-continuous daylight in both polar summers, it can be inferred that they spend virtually no time in darkness across an entire year, relative to most other migratory species.**

Paragraph 1 notes near-continuous daylight in each polar summer and concludes the tern gets more daylight yearly than any other creature while “chasing perpetual summer.” Relative scarcity of darkness versus other migrants is a cautious reading of that daylight crown — not a claim of zero night forever, but “virtually no… relative to most.”

**Tip:** Keep the relative hedge; absolute “never dark” would overclaim.

¶1’s daylight ranking supports the relative-darkness inference, so the line holds.

**B) If the average round-trip distance was approximately 70,900 kilometres, and one bird travelled roughly 96,000 kilometres, that bird travelled about 25,100 kilometres further than the population average.**

Paragraph 3 supplies both figures; 96,000 − 70,900 = 25,100. The arithmetic follows the stated totals without inventing a third distance.

**Tip:** When both numbers are explicit, a clean difference is fair game if the statement names both sources.

The gap is exact arithmetic from ¶3’s pair of figures, so the inference stands.

**C) Because researchers cite magnetic sensitivity, solar positioning, and visual landmarks as possible navigation mechanisms, the passage implies exactly one of these three must be solely responsible, to the exclusion of the other two.**

Paragraph 6 lists those cues under “a combination of methods is likely involved,” then notes how hard it is to separate contributions. Sole responsibility for one cue contradicts the combination claim.

**Trap:** A menu of mechanisms is not a single-winner tournament.

It fails: ¶6 points to a combination, not one exclusive controller.

**D) Because the S-shaped migratory path appears linked to prevailing wind patterns, it can be inferred that the birds' route may be shaped partly by energy-efficiency considerations rather than being a purely direct geographic path.**

Paragraph 3 ties the S-shaped Atlantic drift to taking “advantage of favourable prevailing wind patterns” instead of a single direct route. Using favourable winds implies an energy-saving geometry without the text needing the word “efficiency.”

Favourable-wind routing in ¶3 supports a partial energy-efficiency reading, so the inference is fair.

**E) Since other species nest near tern colonies to benefit from their aggression, it can be inferred that Arctic terns' defensive behaviour can produce ecological benefits for neighbouring species, not just for the terns themselves.**

Paragraph 7’s neighbouring species nest close “specifically to benefit from this collective defensive aggression against shared predators.” Shared predator pressure is an ecological upside beyond the terns alone.

¶7’s hitchhiking nesters show spillover benefits, so the inference tracks the passage.
highlights: experiences more daylight over the course of a year than any other creature on Earth, effectively chasing perpetual summer
approximately 70,900 kilometres, though several individual birds were recorded travelling considerably further, with one especially long-ranging bird logging a round-trip of roughly 96,000 kilometres
a combination of methods is likely involved
apparently to take advantage of favourable prevailing wind patterns
deliberately nest close to Arctic tern colonies specifically to benefit from this collective defensive aggression against shared predators

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Statements require linking details across the passage in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The technological limitation described in Paragraph 2 (too small for conventional trackers) helps explain why the migration's true extent, described in Paragraph 3, remained uncertain for so long.

Because the 2010 geolocator study revealed distances greater than earlier estimates, and the average round-trip was found to be approximately 70,900 kilometres, the passage implies pre-2010 estimates had significantly overstated the migration's true length.
The mid-journey stopover described in Paragraph 5 is presented as unrelated to the birds' overall energy needs for completing the remainder of their migration.
The partial understanding of navigation mechanisms (Paragraph 6) is consistent with the passage's closing framing of the terns' climate-change response as still uncertain (Paragraph 9).

The birds' dependence on multiple, widely separated stopover points (Paragraph 8) helps explain why disruption to migration might be difficult to detect from a single monitoring location, as stated in the same paragraph.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The technological limitation described in Paragraph 2 (too small for conventional trackers) helps explain why the migration's true extent, described in Paragraph 3, remained uncertain for so long.**

Paragraph 2 says decades of route-and-distance work stayed “largely a matter of estimation” because conventional gear was too heavy; paragraph 3 then shows geolocator data “considerably longer than earlier estimates.” The size barrier is the bridge between weak prior numbers and the 2010 revision.

¶2’s tracker limit causally frames ¶3’s surprise distances, so the synthesis holds.

**B) Because the 2010 geolocator study revealed distances greater than earlier estimates, and the average round-trip was found to be approximately 70,900 kilometres, the passage implies pre-2010 estimates had significantly overstated the migration's true length.**

Paragraph 3 says the migration was “considerably longer than earlier estimates had suggested” — earlier figures were too short, not too long. “Overstated” reverses that direction while keeping the average intact.

**Trap:** “Different from earlier estimates” still needs you to check whether estimates were high or low.

It fails: ¶3 has earlier estimates understating length, so “overstated” is the wrong arrow.

**C) The mid-journey stopover described in Paragraph 5 is presented as unrelated to the birds' overall energy needs for completing the remainder of their migration.**

Paragraph 5 says birds pause apparently “to replenish fat reserves before continuing the remainder of their journey.” Unrelated to energy needs is the opposite of that purpose clause.

**Trap:** “Intriguing detour” can sound optional; the text links it to fat for the remaining legs.

It fails against ¶5’s fat-reserve stopover purpose — energy is the point, not a side note.

**D) The partial understanding of navigation mechanisms (Paragraph 6) is consistent with the passage's closing framing of the terns' climate-change response as still uncertain (Paragraph 9).**

Paragraph 6 leaves navigation “only partially understood”; paragraph 9 leaves climate adjustment versus vulnerability “actively being investigated.” Both chapters refuse a finished scientific map of the species’ limits.

Open questions in ¶6 and ¶9 rhyme as unfinished science, so the cross-link stands.

**E) The birds' dependence on multiple, widely separated stopover points (Paragraph 8) helps explain why disruption to migration might be difficult to detect from a single monitoring location, as stated in the same paragraph.**

Paragraph 8 itself chains the two ideas: dependence on “multiple, widely separated stopover points” across hemispheres, then consequences “difficult to detect from any single monitoring location alone.” The statement restates that in-paragraph causal hinge.

¶8 supplies both the multi-stop dependency and the single-site detection problem, so the synthesis matches.
highlights: the exact route and total distance of this migration remained largely a matter of estimation, since the birds are too small and light to carry conventional tracking equipment
a migration considerably longer than earlier estimates had suggested
apparently using the stopover to replenish fat reserves before continuing the remainder of their journey
remain only partially understood
consequences that might be difficult to detect from any single monitoring location alone

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.exam_title: Grammar Rules (New Sentences, Anchored in Text Vocabulary)
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "Had researchers not developed lighter geolocators, the terns' true migratory route might never have been confirmed."
"The team recommended that future studies tracks a larger sample of birds."
"The number of tracked individuals continue to grow as technology improves."
"Neither the wind patterns nor the food availability were fully predictable at every stopover."
"Having replenished its fat reserves, the bird resumed its journey southward."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Had researchers not developed lighter geolocators, the terns' true migratory route might never have been confirmed."**

This is a clean third-conditional inversion: Had + subject + past participle stands in for If researchers had not…, paired with might never have been confirmed for the unreal past result. Auxiliaries and participle forms line up.

Inverted Had…not + might never have been is sound third-conditional patterning, so the sentence stands.

**B) "The team recommended that future studies tracks a larger sample of birds."**

After recommend that, exam English wants the present subjunctive — base form track, not tracks. Future studies is plural, but the real fault is subjunctive, not mere agreement.

**Trap:** Plural subject + -s looks like ordinary present; recommend that drops the -s anyway.

Recommend that needs base-form track, so this fails — "The team recommended that future studies track a larger sample of birds."

**C) "The number of tracked individuals continue to grow as technology improves."**

The number of is a singular head; the plural noun after of does not control the verb. Continue should be continues.

**Trap:** Do not let individuals (plural) pull the verb — number is the true subject.

Singular the number of needs continues, so the line fails — "The number of tracked individuals continues to grow as technology improves."

**D) "Neither the wind patterns nor the food availability were fully predictable at every stopover."**

With neither…nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. Food availability is singular, so were should be was. Treating the pair as a plural set still does not override nearest-noun agreement in exam English.

**Trap:** A plural first noun (wind patterns) often tricks writers into were even when nor lands on a singular.

Nearest-subject agreement wants was, so the wording fails — "Neither the wind patterns nor the food availability was fully predictable at every stopover."

**E) "Having replenished its fat reserves, the bird resumed its journey southward."**

The perfect participle Having replenished correctly marks fueling before resumption, and its / the bird keeps the same referents — no dangling modifier. Sequence and agreement are clean.

Same-subject participle plus past resumed is well formed, so the sentence stands.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "No sooner had the birds reached the stopover than they began feeding intensively."
"The migration route, along with several recorded detours, were mapped in detail."
"Each of the tracked terns have followed a broadly similar seasonal pattern."
"By the time the birds reach Antarctica, they will have already flown tens of thousands of kilometres."
"The data, which were collected using miniaturised geolocators, reveal a far longer migration than expected."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "No sooner had the birds reached the stopover than they began feeding intensively."**

No sooner…than correctly forces inversion (had before the subject) and pairs past perfect with a simple-past follow-on. Than (not when) is the right linker.

**Tip:** Front the auxiliary: No sooner had…, not No sooner the birds had…

Inverted No sooner had…than… is textbook form, so the sentence stands.

**B) "The migration route, along with several recorded detours, were mapped in detail."**

Along with… is a parenthetical add-on; the grammatical subject remains singular migration route. Were should be was.

**Trap:** Material after along with / as well as / together with does not make a singular head plural.

Singular route controls the verb, so this fails — "The migration route, along with several recorded detours, was mapped in detail."

**C) "Each of the tracked terns have followed a broadly similar seasonal pattern."**

Each of takes a singular verb even when of is followed by a plural noun. Have followed should be has followed.

**Trap:** Terns (plural) sits next to the verb and tempts have; each still rules.

Each of needs has followed, so the line fails — "Each of the tracked terns has followed a broadly similar seasonal pattern."

**D) "By the time the birds reach Antarctica, they will have already flown tens of thousands of kilometres."**

By the time + present reach sets a future boundary; will have already flown is future perfect for miles completed before that arrival. The aspect matches the deadline.

Future perfect after by the time fits completed flight before arrival, so the wording stands.

**E) "The data, which were collected using miniaturised geolocators, reveal a far longer migration than expected."**

Here data is treated as plural: were collected in the relative clause and reveal in the main clause agree. Consistent plural handling is acceptable exam English for scientific data.

Plural data with were / reveal stays consistent, so the sentence stands.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "Despite of the logistical challenges, researchers successfully tracked several breeding pairs."
"Whoever analyses the tracking data should account for individual variation between birds."
"The team denied having deliberately overstated the average migration distance."
"There is several mechanisms that likely contribute to the terns' navigation."
"The colony, which was studied over several breeding seasons, showed consistent defensive behaviour."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Despite of the logistical challenges, researchers successfully tracked several breeding pairs."**

Despite never takes of; the of belongs to the twin phrase in spite of. Either drop of after despite or switch to in spite of.

**Trap:** Despite of is a high-frequency blend of despite + in spite of.

Despite of is ungrammatical, so the line fails — "Despite the logistical challenges, researchers successfully tracked several breeding pairs."

**B) "Whoever analyses the tracking data should account for individual variation between birds."**

Whoever is a free relative meaning “the person who,” correctly heading the subject clause; analyses (BrE singular) and should account are well formed.

Whoever as clausal subject with a matching singular verb is sound, so the sentence stands.

**C) "The team denied having deliberately overstated the average migration distance."**

Deny + perfect gerund (having overstated) correctly places the alleged overstatement before the denial. Deliberately is a clean adverb inside the gerund phrase.

Denied having + past participle is the right pattern for a prior act, so the wording stands.

**D) "There is several mechanisms that likely contribute to the terns' navigation."**

Existential there agrees with the real subject that follows; several mechanisms is plural, so is must become are.

**Trap:** There is feels fixed; always check the noun after it.

Plural mechanisms need There are, so this fails — "There are several mechanisms that likely contribute to the terns' navigation."

**E) "The colony, which was studied over several breeding seasons, showed consistent defensive behaviour."**

The non-defining which-clause agrees with singular colony (was studied), and the main verb showed likewise stays singular. Punctuation and agreement are tidy.

Singular colony with was / showed is consistent, so the sentence stands.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly written, using a word or phrase echoing the passage's vocabulary. Decide if the word/phrase is used correctly according to its established meaning.
statements: "A geolocator is a small device used to record and transmit an animal's approximate location over time."
"Prevailing wind patterns refers to the specific winds that occur only once, on a single unrepeated occasion."
"A stopover, in migratory biology, refers to a site where travelling animals pause to rest and replenish energy reserves."
"Olfactory cues refers to information gathered through an animal's sense of smell."
"A breeding colony refers to a group of animals that reproduce and nest together in the same area."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "A geolocator is a small device used to record and transmit an animal's approximate location over time."**

That matches how the passage’s 2010 tags work: tiny devices that let movements be “tracked in detail.” Location-logging over time is the established sense, not a navigational compass itself.

The definition fits standard scientific use (and ¶2’s trackers), so the wording is sound.

**B) "Prevailing wind patterns refers to the specific winds that occur only once, on a single unrepeated occasion."**

Prevailing means dominant or usual over a period — the opposite of a one-off gust. Paragraph 3’s “favourable prevailing wind patterns” are habitual routes, not single-event winds.

**Trap:** Sounding like “the winds that prevail today” can be twisted into “once only”; the adjective means typically dominant.

Once-only winds invert prevailing’s meaning, so this use fails.

**C) "A stopover, in migratory biology, refers to a site where travelling animals pause to rest and replenish energy reserves."**

That is the standard migratory sense, and paragraph 5’s Greenland pause to “replenish fat reserves” is exactly that kind of site. Rest-and-refuel, not permanent residence.

Stopover as a refueling pause matches established migratory usage, so the definition stands.

**D) "Olfactory cues refers to information gathered through an animal's sense of smell."**

Olfactory = smell-related; cues are sensory signals. Paragraph 6 lists “possibly olfactory cues” beside visual landmarks as candidate navigation inputs — smell-based information, not taste or sound.

Smell-based information is the right sense of olfactory cues, so the wording stands.

**E) "A breeding colony refers to a group of animals that reproduce and nest together in the same area."**

That is the ordinary biology sense; paragraph 7’s “Breeding colonies” that dive-bomb intruders are communal nesting groups, not solitary nests.

Communal breed-and-nest group matches breeding colony, so the definition is sound.
highlights: favourable prevailing wind patterns
visual landmarks and possibly olfactory cues

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly written, using a word or phrase echoing the passage. Decide if the word/ phrase is used correctly according to its established meaning.
statements: "Dive-bombing, as a defensive behaviour, refers to a bird making a fast, aggressive downward attack toward a threat."
"A round-trip distance refers to the total distance travelled in only one direction, excluding the return journey."
"Perpetual summer, as used figuratively here, refers to continuously experiencing summer-like daylight conditions by moving between hemispheres."
"Logistical constraints refers to practical difficulties that make carrying out a plan or experiment more difficult."
"A monitoring location refers to a fixed point from which researchers observe and record data over time."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Dive-bombing, as a defensive behaviour, refers to a bird making a fast, aggressive downward attack toward a threat."**

That matches ordinary bird-behaviour use and paragraph 7’s colonies that “collectively dive-bomb intruders,” striking heads with bills. Fast downward aggression toward a threat is exact.

Defensive downward attack is the right sense, so the wording stands.

**B) "A round-trip distance refers to the total distance travelled in only one direction, excluding the return journey."**

Round-trip means out and back combined. Paragraph 3’s “average round-trip distance” and the 96,000 km “round-trip” are full migrations, not one-way legs. Excluding the return flips the meaning.

**Trap:** Round can tempt “one circuit in one direction”; the compound still includes the return.

One-way-only denies round-trip’s out-and-back sense, so this use fails.

**C) "Perpetual summer, as used figuratively here, refers to continuously experiencing summer-like daylight conditions by moving between hemispheres."**

Paragraph 1’s “effectively chasing perpetual summer between hemispheres” is figurative daylight strategy, not literal endless calendar summer in one place. The gloss tracks that metaphor.

Chasing daylight summers across hemispheres matches ¶1’s figurative perpetual summer, so the wording stands.

**D) "Logistical constraints refers to practical difficulties that make carrying out a plan or experiment more difficult."**

Logistics = practical organisation of a task; constraints are limiting factors. Paragraph 6 cites “obvious logistical constraints” on ocean-crossing navigation experiments — feasibility barriers, not theoretical ones.

Practical feasibility limits fit logistical constraints, so the definition stands.

**E) "A monitoring location refers to a fixed point from which researchers observe and record data over time."**

That is standard field-science sense; paragraph 8’s worry that disruption may be “difficult to detect from any single monitoring location alone” assumes fixed watchpoints gathering observations.

A fixed observational site matches monitoring location, so the wording is sound.
highlights: collectively dive-bomb intruders
The average round-trip distance recorded across the tracked population was approximately 70,900 kilometres
effectively chasing perpetual summer between hemispheres
poses obvious logistical constraints
difficult to detect from any single monitoring location alone

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The Wright brothers' first flight covered approximately 37 metres in about 12 seconds, at a top speed of roughly 48 kilometres per hour.
The First World War is described as having transformed aviation into a strategically significant military technology.
Piston engines are described as having offered unlimited power-to-weight ratios, unconstrained by any technological limitation.
Lindbergh's 1927 transatlantic flight covered approximately 5,800 kilometres in roughly 33.5 hours.
By the late 1920s, cruising speeds for advanced aircraft are described as having increased to more than ten times the speed achieved at Kitty Hawk.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The Wright brothers' first flight covered approximately 37 metres in about 12 seconds, at a top speed of roughly 48 kilometres per hour.**

Paragraph 1 pins down the Kitty Hawk hop with exact figures: "just 37 metres in approximately 12 seconds" and "a top speed of roughly 48 kilometres per hour." The statement simply restates those quantities without stretching them.

**Tip:** When several numbers sit in one paragraph, check each figure against the same sentence cluster rather than mixing later decades.

The distance, duration, and speed all match Paragraph 1, so the claim is true.

**B) The First World War is described as having transformed aviation into a strategically significant military technology.**

Paragraph 2 says the outbreak of the First World War "transformed aviation from a fragile novelty into a strategically significant military technology." That is an explicit causal claim, not an inference you have to invent.

Wartime development is framed as the hinge that made aviation strategically important, so the statement is true.

**C) Piston engines are described as having offered unlimited power-to-weight ratios, unconstrained by any technological limitation.**

Paragraph 2 says the opposite: aircraft "remained fundamentally limited by the relatively low power-to-weight ratios achievable with early piston engines." "Unlimited" and "unconstrained" invent a capability the text never grants.

**Trap:** Swap "low" or "limited" for unbound praise and the item flips while still sounding technical.

The statement reverses the piston-engine limitation named in Paragraph 2, so it is false.

**D) Lindbergh's 1927 transatlantic flight covered approximately 5,800 kilometres in roughly 33.5 hours.**

Paragraph 3 places Lindbergh's 1927 flight at "approximately 5,800 kilometres… in roughly 33.5 hours." The statement copies those two measurements without changing the year or the route scale.

Both distance and duration match Paragraph 3, so the claim is true.

**E) By the late 1920s, cruising speeds for advanced aircraft are described as having increased to more than ten times the speed achieved at Kitty Hawk.**

Paragraph 3 says cruising speeds rose to roughly 200 km/h, "more than four times the speed achieved at Kitty Hawk" — not ten times. The multiplier is the distortion.

**Trap:** Exam writers often swap a faithful multiple (four) for a flashier one (ten) while keeping the rest of the sentence intact.

The passage caps the gain at more than four times Kitty Hawk's speed, so the "ten times" claim is false.
highlights: just 37 metres in approximately 12 seconds
transformed aviation from a fragile novelty into a strategically significant military technology
remained fundamentally limited by the relatively low power-to-weight ratios achievable with early piston engines
covered approximately 5,800 kilometres between New York and Paris in roughly 33.5 hours
more than four times the speed achieved at Kitty Hawk

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Jet propulsion was first demonstrated in operational military aircraft during the closing years of the Second World War.
The de Havilland Comet's structural failures were later traced to metal fatigue around its window frames.
The Comet's introduction increased typical intercontinental journey times compared to propellerdriven aircraft it replaced.
The Boeing 747 entered commercial service in 1969, capable of carrying more than 400 passengers at cruising speeds exceeding 900 kilometres per hour.
The Boeing 747's entry into service occurred more than 66 years after the Wright brothers' first flight.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Jet propulsion was first demonstrated in operational military aircraft during the closing years of the Second World War.**

Paragraph 4 dates the first demonstration of practical jet propulsion in "operational military aircraft during the closing years of the Second World War." The statement restates that timing and setting.

The wartime military debut matches Paragraph 4, so the claim is true.

**B) The de Havilland Comet's structural failures were later traced to metal fatigue around its window frames.**

Paragraph 5 attributes the Comet's "catastrophic structural failures" to damage "later traced to metal fatigue around window frames." Cause and location are named directly.

The fatigue diagnosis around the window frames matches Paragraph 5, so the statement is true.

**C) The Comet's introduction increased typical intercontinental journey times compared to propellerdriven aircraft it replaced.**

Paragraph 5 says the Comet cut typical journey times "by roughly half" versus the propeller-driven aircraft it replaced. "Increased" flips the direction of the change.

**Trap:** Direction traps (cut vs increase, half vs double) often leave the rest of the wording untouched.

The passage says times were cut roughly in half, so the "increased" claim is false.

**D) The Boeing 747 entered commercial service in 1969, capable of carrying more than 400 passengers at cruising speeds exceeding 900 kilometres per hour.**

Paragraph 6 packs the same trio: entry "By 1969," "more than 400 passengers," and "cruising speeds exceeding 900 kilometres per hour." The statement gathers those facts without altering them.

Year, capacity, and cruise speed all match Paragraph 6, so the claim is true.

**E) The Boeing 747's entry into service occurred more than 66 years after the Wright brothers' first flight.**

Paragraph 6 clocks the 747's arrival as "less than 66 years after Kitty Hawk," not more than. The comparison word is inverted.

**Trap:** "Less than" versus "more than" on the same number is a classic chronology trap.

The passage says less than 66 years after Kitty Hawk, so the "more than" wording is false.
highlights: first demonstrated in operational military aircraft during the closing years of the Second World War
later traced to metal fatigue around window frames
cutting typical journey times on major intercontinental routes by roughly half compared to the propeller-driven aircraft it replaced
capable of carrying more than 400 passengers across oceans at cruising speeds exceeding 900 kilometres per hour
less than 66 years after Kitty Hawk

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Concorde cruised at speeds exceeding 2,100 kilometres per hour, more than twice the speed of sound.
Concorde is described as having become commercially self-sustaining despite its high operating costs.
Modern wide-body aircraft consume approximately 80% less fuel per passenger-kilometre than aircraft from the 1960s.
Typical cruising speeds are described as having increased substantially since the 1960s, alongside efficiency improvements.
The passage concludes by presenting aviation's future trajectory as a settled question with a clear, agreed-upon answer.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Concorde cruised at speeds exceeding 2,100 kilometres per hour, more than twice the speed of sound.**

Paragraph 7 states that Concorde "cruised at speeds exceeding 2,100 kilometres per hour, more than twice the speed of sound." Both the figure and the Mach comparison are explicit.

Speed and the "more than twice sonic" claim match Paragraph 7, so the statement is true.

**B) Concorde is described as having become commercially self-sustaining despite its high operating costs.**

Paragraph 7 lists high costs, limited seating, and regulatory limits, then says the aircraft "never became commercially self-sustaining." The statement claims the opposite outcome.

**Trap:** Admitting high costs while asserting commercial success looks balanced but contradicts the verdict in the text.

The passage says Concorde never became commercially self-sustaining, so the claim is false.

**C) Modern wide-body aircraft consume approximately 80% less fuel per passenger-kilometre than aircraft from the 1960s.**

Paragraph 8 gives the efficiency figure almost verbatim: modern wide-bodies "consume approximately 80% less fuel per passenger-kilometre than aircraft from the 1960s."

The 80% fuel saving matches Paragraph 8, so the statement is true.

**D) Typical cruising speeds are described as having increased substantially since the 1960s, alongside efficiency improvements.**

Paragraph 8 credits big efficiency gains while saying "typical cruising speeds have remained essentially unchanged since the 1960s." Speed growth is the false half of the claim.

Efficiency improved while cruise speed stayed flat; the "increased substantially" part fails, so the statement is false.

**E) The passage concludes by presenting aviation's future trajectory as a settled question with a clear, agreed-upon answer.**

Paragraph 9 leaves the long-run trajectory as "a question aviation historians and engineers continue to debate," not a settled consensus.

**Trap:** Closing paragraphs often sound decisive; check whether the text actually declares a verdict or only frames a debate.

The ending is an open debate, not an agreed answer, so the statement is false.
highlights: cruised at speeds exceeding 2,100 kilometres per hour, more than twice the speed of sound
never became commercially self-sustaining
consume approximately 80% less fuel per passenger-kilometre than aircraft from the 1960s
typical cruising speeds have remained essentially unchanged since the 1960s
a question aviation historians and engineers continue to debate

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Statements test whether a plausible-sounding inference is actually supported by the passage, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Since the Wright Flyer's speed was roughly 48 km/h and cruising speeds reached roughly 200 km/h by the late 1920s, the increase over that period was approximately 152 km/h in absolute terms.

Because jet engines offered a different power-to-weight relationship than piston engines, it can be inferred that this shift enabled performance levels previously structurally impossible, not merely marginally improved ones.
Because Concorde was retired in 2003, it can be inferred that supersonic commercial flight was technologically infeasible, rather than economically unsustainable.
Since fuel efficiency improved by roughly 80% while cruising speeds stayed flat, it can be inferred that recent aviation progress has been concentrated in efficiency rather than raw speed.
Because the Comet was grounded following structural failures, it can be inferred that jet-powered commercial aviation was permanently abandoned as a result.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Since the Wright Flyer's speed was roughly 48 km/h and cruising speeds reached roughly 200 km/h by the late 1920s, the increase over that period was approximately 152 km/h in absolute terms.**

Paragraph 1 gives ~48 km/h at Kitty Hawk; Paragraph 3 gives ~200 km/h by the late 1920s. Subtracting yields 152 km/h, so the arithmetic inference is licensed by those two figures.

**Tip:** Absolute-difference items are fair when both endpoints are stated; inventing a start or end speed is not.

Both speeds appear in the passage and 200 − 48 = 152, so the inference is true.

**B) Because jet engines offered a different power-to-weight relationship than piston engines, it can be inferred that this shift enabled performance levels previously structurally impossible, not merely marginally improved ones.**

Paragraph 4 says jet engines offered a "fundamentally different relationship between power and weight" and enabled speeds and altitudes "structurally impossible for earlier aircraft designs." That supports a leap beyond marginal improvement.

The "structurally impossible" wording backs the stronger performance claim, so the inference is true.

**C) Because Concorde was retired in 2003, it can be inferred that supersonic commercial flight was technologically infeasible, rather than economically unsustainable.**

Paragraph 7 blames retirement on "Persistently high operating costs, limited seating capacity, and regulatory restrictions," and notes the type flew until 2003. Cost and regulation, not technical impossibility, explain the end.

**Trap:** Retirement date ≠ technological failure — successful operations can still die for commercial reasons.

The text frames economics and regulation, not infeasibility, so this inference is false.

**D) Since fuel efficiency improved by roughly 80% while cruising speeds stayed flat, it can be inferred that recent aviation progress has been concentrated in efficiency rather than raw speed.**

Paragraph 8 opens by saying improvement shifted "away from raw speed and toward efficiency," then backs that with ~80% less fuel per passenger-kilometre and unchanged cruise speeds. The inference restates the paragraph's own axis.

The efficiency-over-speed framing is explicit in Paragraph 8, so the inference is true.

**E) Because the Comet was grounded following structural failures, it can be inferred that jet-powered commercial aviation was permanently abandoned as a result.**

Paragraph 5 says the type was only "temporarily grounded," and Paragraph 6 shows jet commercial flight continuing with the 747. "Permanently abandoned" overreaches a temporary pause.

**Trap:** Temporary grounding language gets inflated into permanent industry exit.

The grounding was temporary and jets continued afterward, so permanent abandonment is false.
highlights: achieved a top speed of roughly 48 kilometres per hour
structurally impossible for earlier aircraft designs to survive
Persistently high operating costs, limited seating capacity, and regulatory restrictions
commercial aviation's central axis of improvement has shifted away from raw speed and toward efficiency
temporarily grounded the type

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Statements require linking details across the passage in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The power-to-weight limitations described in Paragraph 2 help explain why jet propulsion, introduced later in Paragraph 4, represented such a consequential leap forward.

Because Concorde's cruising speed exceeded 2,100 km/h and the Boeing 747's exceeded 900 km/h, Concorde's speed was more than double that of the 747's, consistent with figures given in Paragraphs 6 and 7.
The Comet's early structural failures (Paragraph 5) are presented as having permanently ended commercial jet aviation, contradicting the continued development described in Paragraph 6.
The shift toward efficiency described in Paragraph 8 is consistent with the passage's closing suggestion that aviation's easiest technological gains may already have been captured (Paragraph 9).
Because cruising speeds stagnated after Concorde's retirement, the passage implies no further aviation technology development has occurred since 2003.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The power-to-weight limitations described in Paragraph 2 help explain why jet propulsion, introduced later in Paragraph 4, represented such a consequential leap forward.**

Paragraph 2 stresses piston engines' "relatively low power-to-weight ratios"; Paragraph 4 calls jets a "fundamentally different relationship between power and weight" and the "most consequential single leap." Linking those points is exactly the synthesis the chronology invites.

The piston limit sets up why the jet leap mattered, so the cross-paragraph claim is true.

**B) Because Concorde's cruising speed exceeded 2,100 km/h and the Boeing 747's exceeded 900 km/h, Concorde's speed was more than double that of the 747's, consistent with figures given in Paragraphs 6 and 7.**

Paragraph 6 places the 747 above 900 km/h; Paragraph 7 places Concorde above 2,100 km/h. Dividing those floors (2,100 / 900) is more than 2, so "more than double" follows the stated minima.

**Tip:** Floor comparisons ("exceeding X") still support "more than double" when the smaller floor times two sits below the larger floor.

Both speeds come from the passage and Concorde's exceeds twice the 747's, so the synthesis is true.

**C) The Comet's early structural failures (Paragraph 5) are presented as having permanently ended commercial jet aviation, contradicting the continued development described in Paragraph 6.**

Paragraph 5 only says the Comet was "temporarily grounded" and design standards were reshaped; Paragraph 6 then shows the 747 entering service. Nothing claims commercial jets ended for good.

The text records a temporary pause, not a permanent end to jet aviation, so the claim is false.

**D) The shift toward efficiency described in Paragraph 8 is consistent with the passage's closing suggestion that aviation's easiest technological gains may already have been captured (Paragraph 9).**

Paragraph 8 shows progress pivoting to efficiency after speed plateaued; Paragraph 9 floats the idea that the "easiest gains have already been captured." Those beats harmonize rather than collide.

Efficiency-focused late gains mesh with the "easiest gains already captured" debate, so the synthesis is true.

**E) Because cruising speeds stagnated after Concorde's retirement, the passage implies no further aviation technology development has occurred since 2003.**

Paragraph 8 places the post-Concorde story in fuel, safety, and environmental gains — including ~80% less fuel per passenger-kilometre — not a freeze of all technology. Flat cruise speed is not "no further development."

**Trap:** One stagnant metric (speed) is stretched into a claim that nothing else advanced.

Efficiency and materials kept improving after Concorde, so "no further development" is false.
highlights: remained fundamentally limited by the relatively low power-to-weight ratios achievable with early piston engines
cruising speeds exceeding 900 kilometres per hour
temporarily grounded the type
whose easiest gains have already been captured
Modern wide-body aircraft consume approximately 80% less fuel per passenger-kilometre than aircraft from the 1960s

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.exam_title: Grammar Rules (New Sentences, Anchored in Text Vocabulary)
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "Had jet engines not been developed, commercial aviation would have remained substantially slower for decades longer."
"Engineers recommended that the design undergoes further structural testing before certification."
"The number of transatlantic routes served by jet aircraft continue to expand each decade."
"Neither the engine reliability nor the structural materials were sufficiently advanced in the early 1910s."
"Having identified the source of metal fatigue, engineers redesigned the aircraft's window frames."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Had jet engines not been developed, commercial aviation would have remained substantially slower for decades longer."**

This is a third-conditional counterfactual with optional inversion: Had + past participle stands for If…had not…, and the result clause correctly uses would have + past participle. Auxiliaries and negatives land in the right places.

**Tip:** Inverted Had…not… is exam-safe when the result stays would have + V3.

The inverted third conditional is well formed, so the sentence is true.

**B) "Engineers recommended that the design undergoes further structural testing before certification."**

Recommend that triggers the mandative subjunctive: the verb after that should be the bare base form undergo, not present indicative undergoes. The singular design does not change that rule.

**Trap:** Subject–verb agreement habits can trick you into undergoes after a singular noun — ignore that and keep the base form.

After recommended that you need undergo, so the wording is false — "…that the design undergo…."

**C) "The number of transatlantic routes served by jet aircraft continue to expand each decade."**

The number of… is a singular subject even when the noun after of is plural, so the verb must be continues, not continue. Routes do not control the agreement.

**Trap:** A long plural of-phrase often steals the verb; stay locked on number.

Singular the number needs continues, so the sentence is false — "…continues to expand…."

**D) "Neither the engine reliability nor the structural materials were sufficiently advanced in the early 1910s."**

With neither…nor, the verb typically agrees with the nearer subject. Here the nearer noun is plural structural materials, so were is the right choice.

Proximity agreement with plural materials licenses were, so the sentence is true.

**E) "Having identified the source of metal fatigue, engineers redesigned the aircraft's window frames."**

The -ing clause Having identified… correctly modifies engineers, who both identify and redesign. There is no dangling participle attached to the wrong noun.

The participle attaches to the logical agent engineers, so the sentence is true.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "No sooner had the aircraft entered service than structural concerns began to emerge."
"The airframe, along with several related components, were redesigned after the incident."
"Each of the surveyed engineers have proposed a similar structural fix."
"By the time the aircraft is retired, it will have already flown for several decades."
"The figures, which were compiled across several test flights, indicate consistent fuel savings."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "No sooner had the aircraft entered service than structural concerns began to emerge."**

No sooner…than is a correlative inversion pattern: No sooner + had + subject + past participle, then than + simple past. Both halves are correctly formed here.

**Tip:** Remember the partner is than, not when; and the first clause uses past perfect with inversion.

The No sooner…than inversion is textbook-correct, so the sentence is true.

**B) "The airframe, along with several related components, were redesigned after the incident."**

Along with… is parenthetical; the grammatical subject remains singular the airframe, so the verb should be was redesigned, not were. The plural components do not inherit agreement.

**Trap:** Comma-wrapped companions with along with / as well as look like compound subjects but leave the first noun in charge.

Singular airframe needs was, so the wording is false — "…was redesigned…."

**C) "Each of the surveyed engineers have proposed a similar structural fix."**

Each of… takes a singular verb regardless of the plural noun that follows, so have proposed should be has proposed. Engineers is only the of-phrase.

**Trap:** Plural engineers after each of is a classic lure into have.

Each needs has proposed, so the sentence is false — "…has proposed…."

**D) "By the time the aircraft is retired, it will have already flown for several decades."**

By the time + present (future reference) pairs cleanly with future perfect will have flown for an action completed before that future point. The already fits the completed-before-retirement sense.

Future perfect before a future retirement marker is exact, so the sentence is true.

**E) "The figures, which were compiled across several test flights, indicate consistent fuel savings."**

Plural figures correctly takes were compiled inside the non-restrictive which-clause and plural indicate in the main clause. Relatives and main verbs stay aligned.

Plural agreement holds in both the relative and the main verb, so the sentence is true.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether the given meaning of the underlined word, as it is actually used in the passage, is correctly identified.
statements: As used in Paragraph 2, "novelty" means something new and unfamiliar, here describing aviation's early, fragile status before wartime development.
As used in Paragraph 3, "unimaginable" means extremely easy to predict or anticipate in advance.
As used in Paragraph 5, "absorbed" (in "commercial aviation absorbed this technological leap") means physically consumed as fuel, in a literal chemical sense.
As used in Paragraph 7, "self-sustaining" means capable of continuing to operate profitably without ongoing external financial support.
As used in Paragraph 9, "contingent" means guaranteed to occur regardless of any prior conditions or circumstances.
tactical_explanations:
**A) As used in Paragraph 2, "novelty" means something new and unfamiliar, here describing aviation's early, fragile status before wartime development.**

Paragraph 2 contrasts a "fragile novelty" with later "strategically significant military technology," so novelty names something new and not yet established — not a finished arsenal.

That contextual sense matches "new and unfamiliar," so the meaning is true.

**B) As used in Paragraph 3, "unimaginable" means extremely easy to predict or anticipate in advance.**

Paragraph 3 calls Lindbergh's journey "almost unimaginable" to the Wright brothers: something scarcely conceivable, not something easy to foresee. The proposed gloss flips the word.

**Trap:** Opposite-meaning distractors often keep the surrounding history intact.

Unimaginable means hard to conceive, not easy to predict, so the gloss is false.

**C) As used in Paragraph 5, "absorbed" (in "commercial aviation absorbed this technological leap") means physically consumed as fuel, in a literal chemical sense.**

"Commercial aviation absorbed this technological leap" is figurative: the industry took in and applied the advance. Nothing in the sentence treats fuel chemistry.

**Trap:** Everyday concrete senses of absorb (soak up as fuel) do not fit technological-leap metaphors.

The usage means integrated the leap, not burned fuel, so the literal gloss is false.

**D) As used in Paragraph 7, "self-sustaining" means capable of continuing to operate profitably without ongoing external financial support.**

Paragraph 7 says Concorde "never became commercially self-sustaining" after listing costs, capacity, and regulations — commercial viability without perpetual external support is exactly the failed condition.

The profitable-without-ongoing-subsidy reading fits the commercial frame, so the meaning is true.

**E) As used in Paragraph 9, "contingent" means guaranteed to occur regardless of any prior conditions or circumstances.**

Paragraph 9 speaks of "historically contingent breakthroughs" — gains that depend on particular historical conditions — the opposite of "guaranteed regardless."

Contingent here means dependent on circumstances, so the "guaranteed" gloss is false.
highlights: transformed aviation from a fragile novelty into a strategically significant military technology
a journey that would have been almost unimaginable to the Wright brothers
Commercial aviation absorbed this technological leap with striking speed
never became commercially self-sustaining
a series of specific, historically contingent breakthroughs

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether the given meaning of the underlined word, as it is actually used in the passage, is correctly identified.
statements: As used in Paragraph 1, "sustained" means brief and immediately interrupted, describing a flight that lasted only a fraction of a second.
As used in Paragraph 4, "consequential" means having significant importance or far-reaching effects.
As used in Paragraph 6, "envelope" (in "performance envelope") means a physical paper container used to hold documents.
As used in Paragraph 8, "incremental" means occurring suddenly, in one single large step rather than gradually.
As used in Paragraph 2, "fragile" means strong and highly resistant to damage or failure.
tactical_explanations:
**A) As used in Paragraph 1, "sustained" means brief and immediately interrupted, describing a flight that lasted only a fraction of a second.**

Paragraph 1 praises the first "sustained, controlled flight" lasting about 12 seconds — maintained in the air under control, not instantly cut off after a fraction of a second.

**Trap:** The flight was short by modern standards, but sustained still means kept going, not aborted instantly.

Sustained means maintained over time, so the "immediately interrupted" gloss is false.

**B) As used in Paragraph 4, "consequential" means having significant importance or far-reaching effects.**

Paragraph 4 calls jet propulsion "The most consequential single leap," then explains structural-scale performance gains. Consequential here means weighty in effect, not trivial.

Important / far-reaching matches the leap framing, so the meaning is true.

**C) As used in Paragraph 6, "envelope" (in "performance envelope") means a physical paper container used to hold documents.**

"Performance envelope" is engineering jargon for the range of speeds, altitudes, and capabilities an aircraft can handle — figurative, not stationery.

**Trap:** Everyday paper-envelope senses collide with technical compounds like performance envelope.

The phrase names an operational range, not a paper wrapper, so the gloss is false.

**D) As used in Paragraph 8, "incremental" means occurring suddenly, in one single large step rather than gradually.**

Paragraph 8 credits "decades of incremental improvement" — small, cumulative steps across engine design, aerodynamics, and materials — the opposite of one sudden leap.

Incremental means gradual step-by-step change, so the sudden-single-step gloss is false.

**E) As used in Paragraph 2, "fragile" means strong and highly resistant to damage or failure.**

Paragraph 2 calls early aviation a "fragile novelty," contrasting weakness before wartime strengthening. Fragile means delicate / easily broken, not tough.

Fragile is the opposite of highly damage-resistant, so the gloss is false.
highlights: the first sustained, controlled flight of a powered heavier-than-air aircraft
The most consequential single leap
a scale and performance envelope that would have seemed like pure fantasy
decades of incremental improvement in engine design, aerodynamics, and lightweight composite materials

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether the given meaning of the underlined word, as it is actually used in the passage, is correctly identified.
statements: As used in Paragraph 3, "culminating" means beginning or starting a process, rather than reaching its final or highest point.
As used in Paragraph 5, "catastrophic" means minor and easily corrected without significant consequence.
As used in Paragraph 7, "persistently" means occurring only once, briefly, and then never recurring.
As used in Paragraph 8, "axis" (in "central axis of improvement") means the main focus or primary direction around which change has occurred.
As used in Paragraph 9, "trajectory" means the path or course of development that something follows over time.
tactical_explanations:
**A) As used in Paragraph 3, "culminating" means beginning or starting a process, rather than reaching its final or highest point.**

Paragraph 3 says interwar change was "culminating in Charles Lindbergh's solo transatlantic flight" — Lindbergh is framed as a climax of that period, not its opening shot.

Culminating means reaching a high point, not starting, so the gloss is false.

**B) As used in Paragraph 5, "catastrophic" means minor and easily corrected without significant consequence.**

Paragraph 5 speaks of "catastrophic structural failures" that grounded the type and reshaped industry standards — disastrous scale, not a minor fix.

Catastrophic means disastrously severe, so the "minor" reading is false.

**C) As used in Paragraph 7, "persistently" means occurring only once, briefly, and then never recurring.**

"Persistently high operating costs" means costs that stayed high over time. That ongoing sense contradicts "only once…never recurring."

**Trap:** Intensity words (high costs) can distract from the temporal adverb persistently.

Persistently means continuing over time, so the one-off gloss is false.

**D) As used in Paragraph 8, "axis" (in "central axis of improvement") means the main focus or primary direction around which change has occurred.**

Paragraph 8 says commercial aviation's "central axis of improvement" shifted toward efficiency, safety, and environment — a figurative main direction of change, not a geometric line or physical spindle.

Main-focus / primary-direction matches the figurative axis, so the meaning is true.

**E) As used in Paragraph 9, "trajectory" means the path or course of development that something follows over time.**

Paragraph 9 debates "the century-long trajectory from Kitty Hawk to modern wide-body jets" — the developmental path over time, not a one-off event.

Path-over-time is exactly how trajectory is used, so the meaning is true.

a series of catastrophic structural failures

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension of the passage's opening claims, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The potato was domesticated in the Andean highlands roughly 8,000 years ago from thousands of wild tuber varieties.
Chuño is described as a freeze-drying preservation technique allowing potatoes to be stored for years.
European suspicion of the potato was linked partly to its membership in the nightshade family.
The potato was widely eaten as a staple food throughout Europe almost immediately after its introduction in the 1500s.
Frederick the Great's "Potato Order" was issued in 1756, mandating cultivation in Prussia.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The potato was domesticated in the Andean highlands roughly 8,000 years ago from thousands of wild tuber varieties.**

Paragraph 1 places domestication in the high Andean plateaus of present-day Peru and Bolivia and says indigenous peoples cultivated the potato "from thousands of wild tuber varieties over roughly 8,000 years." The statement keeps place, timescale, and wild-source breadth intact.

**Tip:** Dates and quantities that paraphrase the same span still count as true.

The claim matches the opening origin facts, so it is true.

**B) Chuño is described as a freeze-drying preservation technique allowing potatoes to be stored for years.**

Still in Paragraph 1, the text names chuño as "a freeze-drying process" that "allowed potatoes to be stored for years at high altitude without spoiling." Both the method type and the long storage claim line up.

The statement restates Paragraph 1's definition of chuño, so it is true.

**C) European suspicion of the potato was linked partly to its membership in the nightshade family.**

Paragraph 2 says the plant "belonged to the nightshade family, whose relatives include several toxic species," and that this background helped fuel deep suspicion (and even leprosy blame). The family link is explicit, not invented.

**Tip:** "Linked partly" is weaker than "only cause," so it survives here.

The nightshade link is stated in Paragraph 2, so the claim is true.

**D) The potato was widely eaten as a staple food throughout Europe almost immediately after its introduction in the 1500s.**

Paragraph 2 records introduction in the mid-1500s, then undercuts any "immediate staple" story: "for roughly two centuries it was grown mostly as a curious ornamental rather than widely eaten as food." The statement flips chronology and diet status.

**Trap:** Arrival date ≠ immediate culinary adoption.

The claim fails: the passage says ornamental use dominated for about two centuries, not immediate staple eating.

**E) Frederick the Great's "Potato Order" was issued in 1756, mandating cultivation in Prussia.**

Paragraph 3 states that "Frederick the Great of Prussia issued a formal \"Potato Order\" in 1756 mandating cultivation." Ruler, year, place, and mandatory cultivation all match.

The claim tracks Paragraph 3's dated decree, so it is true.
highlights: cultivated it from thousands of wild tuber varieties over roughly 8,000 years
a freeze-drying process known as chuño, which allowed potatoes to be stored for years
Because the plant belonged to the nightshade family, whose relatives include several toxic species
for roughly two centuries it was grown mostly as a curious ornamental rather than widely eaten as food
Frederick the Great of Prussia issued a formal "Potato Order" in 1756 mandating cultivation

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension of the passage's middle claims, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Potatoes are described as yielding roughly four times as many calories per unit of land as wheat under comparable conditions.
One influential study attributed up to 25% of urban population growth in relevant regions to potato adoption.
The Irish Lumper is described as one of many genetically diverse varieties cultivated in Ireland at the time.
The Great Famine, triggered by Phytophthora infestans, began in 1845.
The famine's death toll and emigration together contributed to an overall population decline of roughly 20–25%.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Potatoes are described as yielding roughly four times as many calories per unit of land as wheat under comparable conditions.**

Paragraph 4 gives the economic appeal in just those terms: potatoes "could yield roughly four times as many calories per unit of land as wheat under comparable conditions." Ratio, comparator, and caveat all survive the paraphrase.

The caloric-yield claim matches Paragraph 4, so it is true.

**B) One influential study attributed up to 25% of urban population growth in relevant regions to potato adoption.**

The same paragraph credits "one influential study attributing up to 25% of urban population growth in those areas to the crop's adoption." Ceiling percentage, urban growth focus, and attribution to the potato remain intact.

The 25% urban-growth attribution is explicit, so the statement is true.

**C) The Irish Lumper is described as one of many genetically diverse varieties cultivated in Ireland at the time.**

Paragraph 5 says much of the rural population was "dependent almost exclusively on a single variety, the Irish Lumper," and that this "genetic uniformity" left the crop vulnerable. The statement invents diversity where the text stresses dangerous sameness.

**Trap:** Naming a variety is not the same as calling it one among many co-equal staples.

The claim fails: Ireland relied almost exclusively on one variety, not a diverse mix.

**D) The Great Famine, triggered by Phytophthora infestans, began in 1845.**

Paragraph 5 names Phytophthora infestans and says it "triggered repeated harvest failures beginning in 1845," producing the famine. Pathogen and start year both appear.

The outbreak-and-date framing matches Paragraph 5, so the statement is true.

**E) The famine's death toll and emigration together contributed to an overall population decline of roughly 20–25%.**

Paragraph 5 pairs roughly 1 million deaths and a further 1 million emigrants, "contributing to an overall population decline of roughly 20–25% within just a few years." The statement keeps the combined demographic result.

The 20–25% decline figure is stated outright, so the claim is true.
highlights: potatoes could yield roughly four times as many calories per unit of land as wheat under comparable conditions
one influential study attributing up to 25% of urban population growth in those areas to the crop's adoption
dependent almost exclusively on a single variety, the Irish Lumper
Phytophthora infestans triggered repeated harvest failures beginning in 1845
contributing to an overall population decline of roughly 20–25% within just a few years

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension of the passage's later claims, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Global potato production today totals approximately 370 million tonnes annually.
The International Potato Center's gene bank in Lima is described as containing more than 4,000 distinct potato varieties.
Cooling a cooked potato is described as converting some of its resistant starch into ordinary digestible starch.
The size of the glycemic-response effect from cooling potatoes is described as consistent and identical across all preparation methods.
The passage concludes by presenting the potato's role in population growth as a genuinely debated question among historians.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Global potato production today totals approximately 370 million tonnes annually.**

Paragraph 6 opens with that exact scale: "Global production today totals approximately 370 million tonnes annually." Volume, annual framing, and approximating hedge all match.

The production total matches Paragraph 6, so the statement is true.

**B) The International Potato Center's gene bank in Lima is described as containing more than 4,000 distinct potato varieties.**

Paragraph 7 says "the International Potato Center in Lima maintains a gene bank containing more than 4,000 distinct potato varieties." Institution, city, and count line up.

The gene-bank figure is stated in Paragraph 7, so the claim is true.

**C) Cooling a cooked potato is described as converting some of its resistant starch into ordinary digestible starch.**

Paragraph 8 runs the chemistry the other way: cooling "converts a portion of its digestible starch into so-called resistant starch." The statement reverses which form becomes which.

**Trap:** Direction flips on technical processes are classic true/false bait.

The claim fails: cooling turns digestible starch into resistant starch, not the reverse.

**D) The size of the glycemic-response effect from cooling potatoes is described as consistent and identical across all preparation methods.**

After noting a possible glycemic lowering, Paragraph 8 adds that "the magnitude of this effect varies considerably depending on preparation method." "Consistent and identical across all" invents uniformity the text denies.

The claim fails: the passage says the effect size varies considerably by preparation method.

**E) The passage concludes by presenting the potato's role in population growth as a genuinely debated question among historians.**

Paragraph 9 ends on open disagreement: whether the potato was a "primary driver" or "merely one contributing factor… remains a genuinely debated question among economic historians." The statement mirrors that unresolved framing.

The closing debate is explicit in Paragraph 9, so the claim is true.

the International Potato Center in Lima maintains a gene bank containing more than 4,000 distinct potato varieties
converts a portion of its digestible starch into so-called resistant starch
the magnitude of this effect varies considerably depending on preparation method
