tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Statements test whether a plausible-sounding inference is actually supported by the passage, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Since potatoes yielded roughly four times the calories per unit of land compared to wheat, it can be inferred that a given plot could support meaningfully more people when planted with potatoes rather than wheat.
If the famine killed roughly 1 million people and a further 1 million emigrated, then approximately 2 million people were removed from Ireland's population through these two combined causes.
Because Parmentier's guarded fields were deliberately left unattended at night, it can be inferred that this was intended to make the crop seem more, not less, valuable to onlookers.
Because the potato offered a higher caloric yield, the passage implies this factor alone fully and conclusively explains all population growth observed in adopting regions.
Since resistant starch passes through the small intestine largely unbroken down, it can be inferred that it behaves differently in digestion than ordinary digestible starch.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Since potatoes yielded roughly four times the calories per unit of land compared to wheat, it can be inferred that a given plot could support meaningfully more people when planted with potatoes rather than wheat.**

Paragraph 4 states the fourfold caloric yield and immediately glosses the consequence: "allowing considerably more people to be fed from the same amount of farmland." The inference is the passage's own next step, not a leap.

**Tip:** When the text itself draws the people-fed consequence, the inference is safe.

The more-people inference follows Paragraph 4's own yield argument, so the statement is true.

**B) If the famine killed roughly 1 million people and a further 1 million emigrated, then approximately 2 million people were removed from Ireland's population through these two combined causes.**

Paragraph 5 gives both figures side by side. Adding them is arithmetic on stated quantities, not a new historical claim. "Removed from Ireland's population" fairly covers deaths plus emigration.

The combined ~2 million figure follows cleanly from the paired Paragraph 5 totals, so the claim is true.

**C) Because Parmentier's guarded fields were deliberately left unattended at night, it can be inferred that this was intended to make the crop seem more, not less, valuable to onlookers.**

Paragraph 3 says fields were "guarded loudly by day while deliberately left unguarded at night, tricking suspicious peasants into believing the crop was valuable enough to steal." Day noise plus night vulnerability is the value signal.

The intentional "look valuable" reading is the text's own motive, so the inference is true.

**D) Because the potato offered a higher caloric yield, the passage implies this factor alone fully and conclusively explains all population growth observed in adopting regions.**

Paragraph 4 attributes only "up to 25%" of urban growth in one study, and Paragraph 9 still treats sole-driver status as debated versus "one contributing factor among several." "Alone… all" overclaims certainty.

**Trap:** A strong contributing cause is not a complete exclusive explanation.

The claim fails: the passage never says yield alone fully explains all growth, and later calls that question debated.

**E) Since resistant starch passes through the small intestine largely unbroken down, it can be inferred that it behaves differently in digestion than ordinary digestible starch.**

Paragraph 8 contrasts digestible starch converted into resistant starch that "passes through the small intestine largely unbroken down," with implications for glycemic response versus a hot, freshly cooked potato. Different digestive behaviour is the point of the contrast.

Different digestive behaviour follows from Paragraph 8's breakdown contrast, so the statement is true.

killed roughly 1 million people through starvation and disease, while a further 1 million emigrated
deliberately left unguarded at night, tricking suspicious peasants into believing the crop was valuable enough to steal
or merely one contributing factor among several simultaneous agricultural and economic changes, remains a genuinely debated question

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Statements require linking details across the passage, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The genetic uniformity created by reliance on the Irish Lumper helps explain why a single pathogen was able to devastate Ireland's food supply so severely.
The vulnerability exposed by the Irish famine is presented as a motivating factor behind the later genetic-diversity preservation efforts described toward the end of the passage.
Because 25% of urban population growth in some regions was attributed to potato adoption, the passage implies the remaining 75% must be entirely unexplained by any other historical factor.
The caloric-yield advantage described earlier in the passage is consistent with the same crop later becoming central to a catastrophic single-variety dependency in Ireland.
Because the gene bank preserves more than 4,000 varieties, the passage implies Ireland's nineteenthcentury food supply relied on a similarly large number of varieties.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The genetic uniformity created by reliance on the Irish Lumper helps explain why a single pathogen was able to devastate Ireland's food supply so severely.**

Paragraph 5 links "almost exclusively" dependence on the Irish Lumper to "genetic uniformity" that "left the crop dangerously vulnerable" when Phytophthora infestans hit. Uniformity → one pathogen can wreck the food base is the passage's causal chain.

The vulnerability synthesis matches Paragraph 5's uniformity–pathogen link, so the statement is true.

**B) The vulnerability exposed by the Irish famine is presented as a motivating factor behind the later genetic-diversity preservation efforts described toward the end of the passage.**

Paragraph 7 opens "Partly in response to the vulnerability so starkly illustrated by the Irish famine," then describes gene-bank work to preserve diversity. Cross-section motive is explicit, not guessed.

The famine-to-gene-bank motivation is stated in Paragraph 7, so the claim is true.

**C) Because 25% of urban population growth in some regions was attributed to potato adoption, the passage implies the remaining 75% must be entirely unexplained by any other historical factor.**

Paragraph 4's study attributes "up to 25%" to potato adoption; it never audits the residual share or declares it unexplained. Treating the leftover as "entirely unexplained" adds a claim the text never makes.

**Trap:** An attributed share does not invent a theory about whatever is left.

The claim fails: the passage says nothing that forces the remaining 75% to be unexplained.

**D) The caloric-yield advantage described earlier in the passage is consistent with the same crop later becoming central to a catastrophic single-variety dependency in Ireland.**

Paragraph 4's fourfold yield advantage explains why potatoes could dominate diets; Paragraph 5 then shows Ireland dependent almost exclusively on one variety for daily calories, with disastrous results. High appeal and extreme reliance belong to the same crop story.

**Tip:** Consistency across sections is not the same as claiming yield caused the famine.

The yield-to-dependency arc fits the passage's middle sections, so the statement is true.

**E) Because the gene bank preserves more than 4,000 varieties, the passage implies Ireland's nineteenthcentury food supply relied on a similarly large number of varieties.**

Paragraph 5 stresses almost exclusive reliance on one variety; Paragraph 7's large modern collection is a corrective response to that vulnerability, not a mirror of nineteenth-century Irish practice. The statement reverses the contrast.

The claim fails: Ireland's crisis came from near single-variety dependence, while the 4,000+ bank is a later diversity safeguard.

Partly in response to the vulnerability so starkly illustrated by the Irish famine

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.exam_title: Grammar Rules (New Sentences, Anchored in Text Vocabulary)
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "Had the pathogen not spread so rapidly, the famine's death toll would likely have been considerably lower."
"Officials recommended that farmers diversifies their planted varieties to reduce future risk."
"The number of preserved potato varieties continue to grow as new specimens are catalogued."
"Neither the soil conditions nor the climate were fully suited to reliable wheat cultivation in that region."
"Having subsisted largely on potatoes as a prisoner, Parmentier later championed the crop publicly."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Had the pathogen not spread so rapidly, the famine's death toll would likely have been considerably lower."**

This is a clean third conditional with subject–auxiliary inversion: Had + past participle in the if-clause, and would have + past participle in the result. No missing auxiliary, no tense mix-up.

**Tip:** Inverted Had… is just If… had… with the if dropped.

The conditional pattern is well formed, so the sentence is grammatically correct.

**B) "Officials recommended that farmers diversifies their planted varieties to reduce future risk."**

After recommend that, English needs the mandative subjunctive (base form): farmers diversify, not diversifies. The -s ending wrongly treats the verb as a present-tense finite form agreeing with farmers.

**Trap:** Recommend/insist/require + that → bare infinitive base form.

The sentence fails: repair to "recommended that farmers diversify…".

**C) "The number of preserved potato varieties continue to grow as new specimens are catalogued."**

The number of is a singular head: the number… continues. Continue agrees with the plural noun varieties instead of with number, which is the classic agreement trap.

The sentence fails: repair to "The number of preserved potato varieties continues to grow…".

**D) "Neither the soil conditions nor the climate were fully suited to reliable wheat cultivation in that region."**

Neither… nor joins a plural noun phrase (the soil conditions) and a singular one (the climate). When one conjunct is plural, plural agreement with were is an accepted choice; the coordinated subjects are treated as a joint unsuitable pair.

**Tip:** Mixed-number neither… nor is contested in pedantic rules, but plural were is standard enough here with a plural first conjunct.

The agreement choice is acceptable, so the sentence is grammatically correct.

**E) "Having subsisted largely on potatoes as a prisoner, Parmentier later championed the crop publicly."**

The -ing absolute Having subsisted… correctly attaches to Parmentier, the subject of the main clause. There is no dangling modifier naming the wrong agent.

The participle and main-clause subject match, so the sentence is grammatically correct.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "No sooner had the blight appeared than harvests began failing across the region."
"The gene bank, along with several partner institutions, were responsible for preserving the collection."
"Each of the surveyed farmers have reported declining yields in recent seasons."
"By the time the famine ended, emigration will have already reshaped the country's population."
"The findings, which were compiled across multiple studies, suggest a meaningful glycemic difference."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "No sooner had the blight appeared than harvests began failing across the region."**

No sooner… than correctly triggers inversion (had the blight appeared) and pairs past perfect with a simple-past sequel (began failing). The correlative pair is complete.

**Tip:** No sooner pairs with than, not when.

The inversion correlative is well formed, so the sentence is grammatically correct.

**B) "The gene bank, along with several partner institutions, were responsible for preserving the collection."**

Along with several partner institutions is an aside, not a second subject for plural agreement. The true subject is singular the gene bank, so the verb should be was responsible.

**Trap:** Along with / as well as / together with does not pluralise a singular head.

The sentence fails: repair to "The gene bank… was responsible…".

**C) "Each of the surveyed farmers have reported declining yields in recent seasons."**

Each of takes a singular verb even when the of-phrase is plural. Have reported wrongly agrees with farmers instead of each.

The sentence fails: repair to "Each of the surveyed farmers has reported…".

**D) "By the time the famine ended, emigration will have already reshaped the country's population."**

By the time the famine ended anchors a past reference point, so the result needs past perfect (had already reshaped). Will have… projects a future-perfect result from now, which clashes with a finished past frame.

The sentence fails: repair to "…emigration had already reshaped…".

**E) "The findings, which were compiled across multiple studies, suggest a meaningful glycemic difference."**

Plural findings correctly takes were compiled in the relative clause and suggest in the main clause. Singular/plural agreement stays consistent throughout.

Subject–verb agreement holds, so the sentence is grammatically correct.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether the given meaning of the underlined word, as it is actually used in the passage, is correctly identified.
statements: As used in Paragraph 1, "domesticated" means bred and cultivated by humans over generations, rather than remaining wild.
As used in Paragraph 2, "suspicion" means confident trust and immediate acceptance, rather than doubt or wariness.
As used in Paragraph 3, "accelerated" means slowed down considerably, rather than sped up.
As used in Paragraph 5, "vulnerable" means resistant to harm or unlikely to be affected by disease.
As used in Paragraph 7, "safeguarding" means deliberately exposing something to greater risk.
tactical_explanations:
**A) As used in Paragraph 1, "domesticated" means bred and cultivated by humans over generations, rather than remaining wild.**

Paragraph 1 uses domesticated for the potato's shift from wild Andean tubers to human cultivation over roughly 8,000 years. That is precisely "bred and cultivated by humans… rather than remaining wild."

The gloss matches Paragraph 1's usage, so the statement is true.

**B) As used in Paragraph 2, "suspicion" means confident trust and immediate acceptance, rather than doubt or wariness.**

Paragraph 2 says the potato "was initially met with deep suspicion" before Europeans blamed nightshade kinship and delayed eating it. Suspicion here is doubt/wariness — the opposite of confident trust.

**Trap:** Vocabulary items often offer the antonym dressed as a definition.

The claimed meaning is inverted, so the statement is false.

**C) As used in Paragraph 3, "accelerated" means slowed down considerably, rather than sped up.**

Paragraph 3 says "Adoption accelerated dramatically during the eighteenth century," describing a ramp-up via government campaigns. Accelerated means sped up, not slowed down.

The antonym gloss fails against Paragraph 3, so the statement is false.

**D) As used in Paragraph 5, "vulnerable" means resistant to harm or unlikely to be affected by disease.**

Paragraph 5 says genetic uniformity "left the crop dangerously vulnerable" to Phytophthora infestans. Vulnerable means exposed to harm, not resistant to it.

The claimed meaning reverses Paragraph 5, so the statement is false.

**E) As used in Paragraph 7, "safeguarding" means deliberately exposing something to greater risk.**

Paragraph 7's gene bank is "safeguarding traits such as disease resistance for future breeding programmes" — protecting desirable traits, not exposing them to risk.

The antonym definition fails, so the statement is false.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether the given meaning of the underlined word, as it is actually used in the passage, is correctly identified.
statements: As used in Paragraph 1, "staple" (in "staple crop") means a basic, regularly consumed food forming a major part of a diet.
As used in Paragraph 5, "reliance" means active avoidance of something, rather than dependence on it.
As used in Paragraph 4, "measurably" means to a degree too small to detect or confirm.
As used in Paragraph 8, "meaningfully" (in "meaningfully lower") means to a degree substantial enough to matter, not negligibly.
As used in Paragraph 5, "uniformity" means a wide, varied range of different forms, rather than sameness.
tactical_explanations:
**A) As used in Paragraph 1, "staple" (in "staple crop") means a basic, regularly consumed food forming a major part of a diet.**

Paragraph 1 contrasts the potato's later status as "a staple crop on nearly every continent" with its Andean origins. Staple crop = basic dietary mainstay, not a rare garnish.

The diet-core gloss matches Paragraph 1, so the statement is true.

**B) As used in Paragraph 5, "reliance" means active avoidance of something, rather than dependence on it.**

Paragraph 5 opens "Ireland's reliance eventually became extreme," then explains almost exclusive dependence on the Irish Lumper. Reliance = dependence; "active avoidance" is the opposite.

The antonym gloss fails, so the statement is false.

**C) As used in Paragraph 4, "measurably" means to a degree too small to detect or confirm.**

Paragraph 4 says population growth "measurably outpaced" comparable regions — i.e., to a detectable, confirmable degree. "Too small to detect" inverts the adverb.

The claimed meaning contradicts Paragraph 4, so the statement is false.

**D) As used in Paragraph 8, "meaningfully" (in "meaningfully lower") means to a degree substantial enough to matter, not negligibly.**

Paragraph 8 says cooling can "meaningfully lower the food's glycemic response," contrasting a non-trivial effect with mere noise, while still allowing preparation-dependent magnitude. Substantial-enough-to-matter is the right reading.

The gloss fits Paragraph 8's glycemic claim, so the statement is true.

**E) As used in Paragraph 5, "uniformity" means a wide, varied range of different forms, rather than sameness.**

Paragraph 5's "genetic uniformity" follows from relying on a single variety and explains vulnerability to one pathogen. Uniformity = sameness, not diversity.

**Trap:** Gene-bank diversity elsewhere does not redefine uniformity here.

The antonym gloss fails against Paragraph 5, so the statement is false.
highlights: Long before it became a staple crop on nearly every continent
Ireland's reliance eventually became extreme
population growth measurably outpaced that of comparable regions
this can meaningfully lower the food's glycemic response
This genetic uniformity left the crop dangerously vulnerable

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Below is one short sentence taken directly from the passage. Each numbered option is a paraphrase claiming to preserve its original meaning. Decide whether each one actually does. Original sentence: "For roughly two centuries it was grown mostly as a curious ornamental rather than widely eaten as food."
statements: For a long stretch of time, the plant was cultivated more as a decorative curiosity than as a common part of people's diets.
For roughly two centuries, the plant was widely eaten as food rather than grown as an ornamental.
The plant was, for a long period, largely dismissed as inedible rather than grown for any purpose at all.
During this period, the plant's decorative appeal outweighed its role as a food source for most people.
The plant was grown almost exclusively as food, with any ornamental use being extremely rare.
tactical_explanations:
**A) For a long stretch of time, the plant was cultivated more as a decorative curiosity than as a common part of people's diets.**

The original says it was "grown mostly as a curious ornamental rather than widely eaten as food" for roughly two centuries. Decorative/curiosity use ahead of dietary use is preserved; only the wording softens.

**Tip:** Faithful paraphrase keeps the same unequal comparison, not just shared keywords.

The paraphrase keeps the ornamental-over-food imbalance, so it is true.

**B) For roughly two centuries, the plant was widely eaten as food rather than grown as an ornamental.**

This swaps both sides of the rather than contrast: food becomes primary, ornamental secondary. That is the reverse of "mostly as a curious ornamental rather than widely eaten."

**Trap:** Keeping the time span while flipping the comparison still fails.

The paraphrase inverts the original contrast, so it is false.

**C) The plant was, for a long period, largely dismissed as inedible rather than grown for any purpose at all.**

The original never claims the potato was thought inedible or unused. It was grown — chiefly as decoration — not abandoned as purposeless. "Inedible" and "for any purpose at all" are smuggled-in distortions.

The paraphrase invents motives and nullity the source sentence lacks, so it is false.

**D) During this period, the plant's decorative appeal outweighed its role as a food source for most people.**

"Decorative appeal outweighed… food source" restates the same ranking as "mostly as a curious ornamental rather than widely eaten as food," without adding inedibility or flipping dominance.

The ranking paraphrase holds, so the statement is true.

**E) The plant was grown almost exclusively as food, with any ornamental use being extremely rare.**

This is a near-total inversion: food becomes almost exclusive, ornamental use rare. The original makes ornamental the majority pattern for about two centuries.

The paraphrase reverses which use dominated, so it is false.
highlights: for roughly two centuries it was grown mostly as a curious ornamental rather than widely eaten as food
for roughly two centuries it was grown mostly as a curious ornamental rather than widely eaten as food
for roughly two centuries it was grown mostly as a curious ornamental rather than widely eaten as food
for roughly two centuries it was grown mostly as a curious ornamental rather than widely eaten as food
for roughly two centuries it was grown mostly as a curious ornamental rather than widely eaten as food

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension of the passage's opening claims, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: TSMC produces more than 90% of the world's most advanced logic chips, defined as those built at or below 7 nanometres.
A leading-edge fabrication plant now costs upward of $20 billion to construct.
Multiple companies worldwide currently manufacture the most advanced deep ultraviolet lithography machines, ensuring no single chokepoint exists for this equipment.
The rising capital cost of advanced fabs is described as making it easier for new companies to enter cutting-edge chip manufacturing.
A single deep ultraviolet lithography machine can cost more than $150 million.
tactical_explanations:
**A) TSMC produces more than 90% of the world's most advanced logic chips, defined as those built at or below 7 nanometres.**

Paragraph 1 names TSMC as producing more than 90% of the world's most advanced logic chips and defines that class as chips built at or below 7 nanometres. The statement restates both the share and the process cutoff without adding or dropping a detail.

**Tip:** When a quantity and a definition travel together, both must match the passage.

The claim lines up with Paragraph 1's figure and definition, so it stands.

**B) A leading-edge fabrication plant now costs upward of $20 billion to construct.**

Paragraph 2 states that constructing a single leading-edge fab now costs upward of $20 billion. The statement only shortens that construction-cost claim; the number and direction ("upward of") are unchanged.

The $20 billion construction floor in Paragraph 2 confirms the line.

**C) Multiple companies worldwide currently manufacture the most advanced deep ultraviolet lithography machines, ensuring no single chokepoint exists for this equipment.**

Paragraph 2 says the opposite: only one company in the world, ASML, currently manufactures the most advanced version of this equipment, creating a second, narrower chokepoint. "Multiple companies" and "no single chokepoint" invert that monopoly.

**Trap:** A true second-chokepoint fact is flipped into a diversified-supply claim.

The statement fails because Paragraph 2 limits advanced DUV lithography manufacture to ASML alone: "Only one company in the world, the Dutch firm ASML, currently manufactures the most advanced version of this equipment."

**D) The rising capital cost of advanced fabs is described as making it easier for new companies to enter cutting-edge chip manufacturing.**

Paragraph 3 ties rising factory capital costs to Moore's Second Law and says those costs make it "progressively harder for new entrants to compete at the cutting edge." "Easier" reverses the directional verb.

**Trap:** Harder → easier is a classic polarity flip on cost barriers.

The claim fails; the passage says rising costs make entry "progressively harder," not easier.

**E) A single deep ultraviolet lithography machine can cost more than $150 million.**

Paragraph 2 states that a single deep ultraviolet lithography machine can cost more than $150 million. The statement copies that price ceiling without changing the equipment type or the figure.

The $150 million machine-cost detail in Paragraph 2 matches the statement.
highlights: produces more than 90% of the world's most advanced logic chips, those built using process technologies at or below 7 nanometres
Constructing a single leading-edge fabrication plant, or "fab," now costs upward of $20 billion
Only one company in the world, the Dutch firm ASML, currently manufactures the most advanced version of this equipment
making it progressively harder for new entrants to compete at the cutting edge
a single deep ultraviolet lithography machine, essential for etching circuit patterns onto silicon wafers, can cost more than $150 million

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension of the passage's middle claims, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The 2020–2021 chip shortage is attributed partly to a slowdown in a relatively narrow category of automotive-grade chips.
This shortage is estimated to have reduced global vehicle production by roughly 11.3 million units.
South Korea's 2021 investment programme is described as being funded exclusively by private companies without any public involvement.
Japan is described as having been the dominant force in global chip production during the 1980s before losing significant market share.
The affected automotive-grade chip category is described as representing a large majority of the overall semiconductor market by value.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The 2020–2021 chip shortage is attributed partly to a slowdown in a relatively narrow category of automotive-grade chips.**

Paragraph 4 opens the shortage discussion with "a production slowdown affecting a relatively narrow category of automotive-grade chips." The statement keeps that causal framing — a narrow automotive-grade category, not the whole market.

Paragraph 4's slowdown description supports the claim.

**B) This shortage is estimated to have reduced global vehicle production by roughly 11.3 million units.**

Paragraph 4 says the disruption ultimately reduced global vehicle production by an estimated 11.3 million units. "Roughly" is a fair hedge around "estimated"; the figure itself is unchanged.

The 11.3 million-unit estimate in Paragraph 4 matches the statement.

**C) South Korea's 2021 investment programme is described as being funded exclusively by private companies without any public involvement.**

Paragraph 5 calls South Korea's 2021 programme a "$450 billion publicprivate investment programme." "Exclusively… private" and "without any public involvement" erase the public half of that label.

**Trap:** Public–private becomes private-only — watch the funding mix.

The claim fails; Paragraph 5 marks the programme as public-private, not private-only: "a $450 billion publicprivate investment programme."

**D) Japan is described as having been the dominant force in global chip production during the 1980s before losing significant market share.**

Paragraph 5 says Japan was "once the dominant force in global chip production during the 1980s before losing significant market share to competitors." The statement restates that rise-and-loss arc without inventing a new ranking today.

The 1980s-dominance-then-loss wording in Paragraph 5 confirms the line.

**E) The affected automotive-grade chip category is described as representing a large majority of the overall semiconductor market by value.**

Paragraph 4 says those automotive-grade chips were "worth a small fraction of the overall semiconductor market." "Large majority" is the inverse of "small fraction."

**Trap:** Small market share ↔ large majority is a quantity swap.

The statement fails; the passage calls the category "worth a small fraction of the overall semiconductor market," not a large majority.
highlights: A production slowdown affecting a relatively narrow category of automotive-grade chips
reducing global vehicle production by an estimated 11.3 million units
a $450 billion publicprivate investment programme in 2021
Japan, once the dominant force in global chip production during the 1980s before losing significant market share to competitors
worth a small fraction of the overall semiconductor market

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension of the passage's later claims, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The "silicon shield" theory suggests Taiwan's indispensability gives other nations incentive to help ensure its security.
Critics of the silicon shield theory argue it could make Taiwan a uniquely tempting target rather than a uniquely protected one.
Chinese chipmakers, as of the early 2020s, are described as having fully closed the technological gap with the industry's cutting edge.
Legacy chips are described as irrelevant to critical everyday products such as cars and medical devices.
The passage concludes by presenting the industry's future concentration as a settled matter with a clear, agreed-upon outcome.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The "silicon shield" theory suggests Taiwan's indispensability gives other nations incentive to help ensure its security.**

Paragraph 6 explains the "silicon shield" idea as theorising that Taiwan's indispensability to global electronics supply chains gives other nations a powerful incentive to help ensure its continued security. The statement strips hedging words but keeps the same protective logic.

The shield theory in Paragraph 6 matches the claim.

**B) Critics of the silicon shield theory argue it could make Taiwan a uniquely tempting target rather than a uniquely protected one.**

Paragraph 6 immediately counters that the same dynamic "could equally be read as making Taiwan a uniquely tempting target rather than a uniquely protected one." The statement is that counterargument almost verbatim.

The critics' target-vs-protected contrast in Paragraph 6 confirms the line.

**C) Chinese chipmakers, as of the early 2020s, are described as having fully closed the technological gap with the industry's cutting edge.**

Paragraph 7 says Chinese manufacturers as of the early 2020s "remained several process-technology generations behind the industry's absolute cutting edge." "Fully closed" contradicts "several… generations behind."

**Trap:** Lag in the text becomes catch-up in the statement.

The claim fails; Paragraph 7 reports Chinese makers "remained several process-technology generations behind," not caught up.

**D) Legacy chips are described as irrelevant to critical everyday products such as cars and medical devices.**

Paragraph 8 says legacy chips "remain critical to everyday products such as cars, appliances, and medical devices." "Irrelevant" flips "critical."

The statement fails; the passage says legacy chips "remain critical" to those products, not irrelevant.

**E) The passage concludes by presenting the industry's future concentration as a settled matter with a clear, agreed-upon outcome.**

Paragraph 9 ends by calling whether diversification will reduce concentration — or economics will keep favouring it — "an open question actively debated among industry analysts and policymakers." "Settled" and "agreed-upon" erase that open debate.

**Trap:** An "open question" is dressed up as a closed conclusion.

The claim fails; Paragraph 9 frames the outcome as "an open question actively debated," not a settled consensus.
highlights: theorising that the island's indispensability to global electronics supply chains gives other nations a powerful incentive to help ensure its continued security
critics counter that this dynamic could equally be read as making Taiwan a uniquely tempting target rather than a uniquely protected one
Chinese manufacturers as of the early 2020s remained several process-technology generations behind the industry's absolute cutting edge
remain critical to everyday products such as cars, appliances, and medical devices
remains an open question actively debated among industry analysts and policymakers

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Statements test whether a plausible-sounding inference is actually supported by the passage, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Since ASML is the sole manufacturer of the most advanced lithography machines, it can be inferred that any country lacking access to ASML's equipment would face significant obstacles reaching the industry's cutting edge.

Because rising fab costs have outpaced transistor-density gains under "Moore's Second Law," it can be inferred that entering cutting-edge manufacturing has become relatively more, not less, difficult over time.

Because the chip shortage's automotive impact was disproportionate to that category's market share, it can be inferred that even a narrow, low-value disruption can produce outsized economic consequences.
Since China has invested billions in domestic chip production, it can be inferred that state investment alone is sufficient to fully replicate decades of accumulated engineering expertise.
Because Japan is subsidising new fabrication facilities, it can be inferred that Japan currently holds the largest share of global advanced chip manufacturing.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Since ASML is the sole manufacturer of the most advanced lithography machines, it can be inferred that any country lacking access to ASML's equipment would face significant obstacles reaching the industry's cutting edge.**

Paragraph 2 calls ASML's monopoly a second, narrower chokepoint layered on TSMC concentration, and the machines are described as essential for etching advanced patterns. If the only maker is ASML, denied access logically blocks the path to the cutting edge.

**Tip:** A named sole supplier of "essential" gear supports a real barrier inference — stay inside that logic, don't invent extra firms.

The inference follows from ASML's sole-maker chokepoint in Paragraph 2, so the statement holds.

**B) Because rising fab costs have outpaced transistor-density gains under "Moore's Second Law," it can be inferred that entering cutting-edge manufacturing has become relatively more, not less, difficult over time.**

Paragraph 3 says capital costs have risen even faster than transistor doubling, "making it progressively harder for new entrants to compete at the cutting edge." "More, not less, difficult" is exactly that progressive-hardening claim.

Moore's Second Law in Paragraph 3 supports the inference that entry has gotten harder over time.

**C) Because the chip shortage's automotive impact was disproportionate to that category's market share, it can be inferred that even a narrow, low-value disruption can produce outsized economic consequences.**

Paragraph 4 stresses a relatively narrow, small-fraction automotive category that still idled lines and cut about 11.3 million vehicles. The mismatch between small market share and huge production damage is the disproportion the statement names.

The narrow-category / outsized-impact pairing in Paragraph 4 backs the inference.

**D) Since China has invested billions in domestic chip production, it can be inferred that state investment alone is sufficient to fully replicate decades of accumulated engineering expertise.**

Paragraph 7 says that despite billions in state investment, China still lagged several generations behind, "illustrating how difficult it is to close this particular technological gap through capital investment alone, without also replicating decades of accumulated engineering expertise." "Sufficient alone" contradicts "not… alone."

**Trap:** Heavy spending in the text is twisted into proof that money is enough.

The inference fails; Paragraph 7 denies that capital alone can replace "decades of accumulated engineering expertise."

**E) Because Japan is subsidising new fabrication facilities, it can be inferred that Japan currently holds the largest share of global advanced chip manufacturing.**

Paragraph 5 says Japan is subsidising new fabs to rebuild capability it allowed to atrophy after losing 1980s dominance. Paragraph 1 already assigns more than 90% of the most advanced logic chips to TSMC in Taiwan — not to Japan. Subsidies for recovery do not equal today's lead.

**Trap:** Policy effort today is mistaken for current market leadership.

The inference fails; leadership sits with TSMC's "more than 90%" share, while Japan is described as rebuilding lost ground.
highlights: Only one company in the world, the Dutch firm ASML, currently manufactures the most advanced version of this equipment, creating a second, narrower chokepoint layered on top of the first
the capital cost of the factories needed to manufacture those increasingly dense chips has risen even faster, making it progressively harder for new entrants to compete at the cutting edge

worth a small fraction of the overall semiconductor market, nonetheless forced automakers worldwide to idle assembly lines, ultimately reducing global vehicle production by an estimated 11.3 million units
without also replicating decades of accumulated engineering expertise
produces more than 90% of the world's most advanced logic chips

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Statements require linking details across the passage, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The extreme cost and complexity described early in the passage help explain why so few countries or companies can realistically compete at the industry's cutting edge.
The chip shortage's disproportionate impact on vehicle production is consistent with the later point that even legacy, technologically unremarkable chips can cause significant disruption.
Because South Korea and Japan are both investing in domestic capacity, the passage implies these efforts have already fully resolved the industry's underlying geographic concentration.

The "silicon shield" theory and the critics' counterargument together illustrate that Taiwan's chip dominance carries genuinely contested strategic implications, not a single agreed-upon interpretation.

Because China remains several generations behind despite heavy investment, this is consistent with the earlier point that capital cost alone does not guarantee competitive success at the cutting edge.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The extreme cost and complexity described early in the passage help explain why so few countries or companies can realistically compete at the industry's cutting edge.**

Paragraphs 2–3 stack $20 billion fabs, $150 million lithography tools, a single ASML supplier, and Moore's Second Law capital barriers. Those early obstacles are precisely why new entrants struggle at the cutting edge without government-scale backing.

The early cost-and-complexity stack explains the scarcity of cutting-edge competitors, so the synthesis holds.

**B) The chip shortage's disproportionate impact on vehicle production is consistent with the later point that even legacy, technologically unremarkable chips can cause significant disruption.**

Paragraph 4's automotive shortage hit hard despite a small market slice; Paragraph 8 then notes that even legacy chips remain critical and that disruptions need not involve cutting-edge tech to produce outsized consequences. Both scenes show modest-looking chip classes punching above their technological or market profile.

Linking Paragraph 4's outsized hit to Paragraph 8's legacy-chip warning is a fair cross-section read.

**C) Because South Korea and Japan are both investing in domestic capacity, the passage implies these efforts have already fully resolved the industry's underlying geographic concentration.**

Paragraph 5 reports the investment moves, but Paragraph 9 still leaves whether diversification will reduce concentrated vulnerabilities an "open question actively debated." "Already fully resolved" jumps past that undecided ending.

**Trap:** Announced policy is treated as a finished fix.

The synthesis fails; Paragraph 9 keeps the outcome an open question, not a resolved one.

**D) The "silicon shield" theory and the critics' counterargument together illustrate that Taiwan's chip dominance carries genuinely contested strategic implications, not a single agreed-upon interpretation.**

Paragraph 6 presents both the protective "silicon shield" reading and the critics' "tempting target" counter. Setting theory and rebuttal side by side signals contested meaning, not consensus.

The paired theory-and-critique in Paragraph 6 supports a contested-implications reading.

**E) Because China remains several generations behind despite heavy investment, this is consistent with the earlier point that capital cost alone does not guarantee competitive success at the cutting edge.**

Paragraph 3 says rising capital costs make cutting-edge entry progressively harder without government-scale backing and, by implication, more than money. Paragraph 7 shows China still generations behind despite billions, needing decades of engineering expertise too. The later lag illustrates the earlier capital-is-not-enough barrier.

China's lag under heavy spending lines up with the earlier capital-barrier logic, so the synthesis holds.
highlights: Constructing a single leading-edge fabrication plant, or "fab," now costs upward of $20 billion

legacy chips manufactured using older process nodes, remain critical to everyday products such as cars, appliances, and medical devices, meaning that supply disruptions need not involve cutting-edge technology at all to produce outsized economic consequences
remains an open question actively debated among industry analysts and policymakers
critics counter that this dynamic could equally be read as making Taiwan a uniquely tempting target rather than a uniquely protected one
illustrating how difficult it is to close this particular technological gap through capital investment alone, without also replicating decades of accumulated engineering expertise

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.exam_title: Grammar Rules (New Sentences, Anchored in Text Vocabulary)
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "Had the shortage not disrupted automotive supply chains, vehicle production would have remained substantially higher."
"Regulators recommended that the company diversifies its supplier base to reduce risk."
"The number of countries subsidising domestic fabs continue to increase each year."
"Neither the equipment nor the expertise required were easily replicated by new entrants."
"Having invested heavily in domestic capacity, the government sought greater supply chain independence."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Had the shortage not disrupted automotive supply chains, vehicle production would have remained substantially higher."**

This is a third conditional with subject–auxiliary inversion: Had + past participle replaces If… had. The result clause correctly uses would have + past participle (would have remained). The negation sits on the inverted had-clause without breaking the pattern.

**Tip:** Inverted Had… not… pairs with would have + V3 — same timeline as If… had not…

The conditional architecture is sound, so the sentence stands.

**B) "Regulators recommended that the company diversifies its supplier base to reduce risk."**

After recommend that, formal English wants the mandative subjunctive — base form diversify, not present-tense diversifies. The -s ending treats the verb as an ordinary present instead of a subjunctive.

**Trap:** Recommend that + indicative -s is a frequent near-miss.

The line fails; the repaired wording is "Regulators recommended that the company diversify its supplier base to reduce risk."

**C) "The number of countries subsidising domestic fabs continue to increase each year."**

The number of is grammatically singular, so the verb must be continues, not plural continue. The plural countries after of does not control agreement.

**Trap:** A plural noun after of does not make "the number of" plural.

Agreement breaks here; the sound version is "The number of countries subsidising domestic fabs continues to increase each year."

**D) "Neither the equipment nor the expertise required were easily replicated by new entrants."**

With neither… nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. Here that subject is the expertise required — singular uncountable expertise — so the verb should be was, not were.

**Trap:** Two nouns before the verb tempt a plural even when the nearer head is singular.

Proximity agreement fails, so the sentence doesn’t hold — "Neither the equipment nor the expertise required was easily replicated by new entrants."

**E) "Having invested heavily in domestic capacity, the government sought greater supply chain independence."**

The perfect participle Having invested modifies the government, the same agent that sought independence afterward. No dangling or mismatched subject — the investor and the seeker are one.

The participle attaches cleanly to the government, so the wording is sound.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "No sooner had the shortage begun than automakers started idling assembly lines."
"The programme, along with several related subsidies, were announced the same year."
"Each of the surveyed manufacturers have reported ongoing supply constraints."
"By the time the new fab opens, competitors will have already expanded their own capacity."
"The figures, which were compiled across several fiscal years, indicate a persistent cost increase."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "No sooner had the shortage begun than automakers started idling assembly lines."**

No sooner… than correctly triggers inversion (had the shortage begun) with past perfect in the first clause and simple past (started) in the second. The correlative pair is than, not when.

**Tip:** No sooner + inversion wants than, and past perfect before the simple-past follow-on.

The No sooner… than pattern is well formed, so the sentence stands.

**B) "The programme, along with several related subsidies, were announced the same year."**

Along with several related subsidies is a parenthetical add-on; the real subject is singular the programme, so the verb must be was announced, not were. The plural noun inside the aside does not take over agreement.

**Trap:** Along with + plural looks like a plural subject, but the head noun still governs the verb.

Agreement fails; repair to "The programme, along with several related subsidies, was announced the same year."

**C) "Each of the surveyed manufacturers have reported ongoing supply constraints."**

Each of takes a singular verb even when the of-phrase is plural. Have reported should be has reported.

**Trap:** Manufacturers after of invites plural have, but Each keeps the verb singular.

The plural verb after Each is wrong — "Each of the surveyed manufacturers has reported ongoing supply constraints."

**D) "By the time the new fab opens, competitors will have already expanded their own capacity."**

By the time + present (opens) sets a future reference point; will have expanded is future perfect for completion before that point. Already sits naturally inside the perfect.

Future perfect before a future By the time marker is the right tense pairing, so the line holds.

**E) "The figures, which were compiled across several fiscal years, indicate a persistent cost increase."**

Plural figures takes were compiled in the non-restrictive which-clause and plural indicate in the main clause. Relative and main verbs both track the same plural head.

Plural subject and plural verbs align throughout, so the sentence is sound.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether the given meaning of the underlined word, as it is actually used in the passage, is correctly identified.
statements: As used in Paragraph 1, "reckless" means carefully considered and prudent, rather than dangerously risky.
As used in Paragraph 2, "chokepoint" means a critical point of vulnerability where disruption could severely restrict an entire system.
As used in Paragraph 5, "atrophy" means to strengthen and grow steadily over time.
As used in Paragraph 6, "indispensability" means the quality of being easily replaced or unnecessary.
As used in Paragraph 8, "outsized" means smaller than would normally be expected.
tactical_explanations:
**A) As used in Paragraph 1, "reckless" means carefully considered and prudent, rather than dangerously risky.**

Paragraph 1 says such geographic concentration "would be considered reckless in almost any other critical industry." There reckless means dangerously unwise or unduly risky — the opposite of carefully considered and prudent.

**Trap:** A negative evaluative word is glossed as its positive antonym.

The gloss fails; in Paragraph 1 reckless means dangerously risky, not prudent.

**B) As used in Paragraph 2, "chokepoint" means a critical point of vulnerability where disruption could severely restrict an entire system.**

Paragraph 2 calls ASML's monopoly "a second, narrower chokepoint layered on top of the first," after describing essential lithography gear only one firm can make. That usage matches a critical vulnerability node whose disruption can bottleneck a whole supply chain.

The Paragraph 2 sense of chokepoint matches the offered meaning, so the identification holds.

**C) As used in Paragraph 5, "atrophy" means to strengthen and grow steadily over time.**

Paragraph 5 says Japan is trying to rebuild capability "it had allowed to atrophy." Allowed to atrophy means allowed to wither or weaken from disuse — not strengthen and grow.

The gloss reverses the verb; atrophy here means weaken from neglect, so the meaning claim fails.

**D) As used in Paragraph 6, "indispensability" means the quality of being easily replaced or unnecessary.**

Paragraph 6 speaks of "the island's indispensability to global electronics supply chains" as the basis of a silicon-shield theory. Indispensability means being essential / hard to do without — the opposite of easily replaced or unnecessary.

The antonym gloss collapses; indispensability here means essentialness, not replaceability.

**E) As used in Paragraph 8, "outsized" means smaller than would normally be expected.**

Paragraph 8 says disruptions need not involve cutting-edge tech "to produce outsized economic consequences." Outsized means disproportionately large, not smaller than expected.

**Trap:** Out- as a size prefix is misread as undersized.

The meaning claim fails; outsized here means larger than normal, not smaller.
highlights: creating a level of geographic concentration that would be considered reckless in almost any other critical industry
creating a second, narrower chokepoint layered on top of the first
rebuild capability it had allowed to atrophy
the island's indispensability to global electronics supply chains
to produce outsized economic consequences

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether the given meaning of the underlined word, as it is actually used in the passage, is correctly identified.
statements: As used in Paragraph 3, "cutting-edge" means outdated or technologically behind current standards.
As used in Paragraph 4, "idle" (as in "idle assembly lines") means to keep running continuously at full capacity.
As used in Paragraph 7, "replicating" means copying or reproducing something that already exists elsewhere.
As used in Paragraph 8, "unremarkable" means ordinary or unexceptional, not attracting special notice.
As used in Paragraph 9, "concentration" (in this economic sense) means being spread evenly and widely across many locations.
tactical_explanations:
**A) As used in Paragraph 3, "cutting-edge" means outdated or technologically behind current standards.**

Paragraph 3 talks about competing "at the cutting edge" of chip manufacturing after describing denser, more expensive fabs. Cutting-edge means at the technological forefront — the opposite of outdated or behind.

The gloss fails; cutting-edge here means leading-tech, not behind the curve.

**B) As used in Paragraph 4, "idle" (as in "idle assembly lines") means to keep running continuously at full capacity.**

Paragraph 4 says the shortage "forced automakers worldwide to idle assembly lines," then cut vehicle output by millions. Idle here means shut down or leave unused — not run at full capacity.

**Trap:** Everyday "idle" as "not working" is flipped into continuous full production.

The claimed meaning reverses the verb; idle here means stop or pause the lines, so the identification fails.

**C) As used in Paragraph 7, "replicating" means copying or reproducing something that already exists elsewhere.**

Paragraph 7 says closing the gap needs more than capital, "without also replicating decades of accumulated engineering expertise." Replicating there means copying / reproducing that expertise — matching the offered gloss.

The Paragraph 7 use of replicating matches "copying or reproducing," so the meaning holds.

**D) As used in Paragraph 8, "unremarkable" means ordinary or unexceptional, not attracting special notice.**

Paragraph 8 calls older-node chips "technologically unremarkable by industry standards" — ordinary relative to the cutting edge, not specially impressive. That is ordinary / unexceptional.

Unremarkable in Paragraph 8 means ordinary, so the identification stands.

**E) As used in Paragraph 9, "concentration" (in this economic sense) means being spread evenly and widely across many locations.**

Paragraph 9 asks whether economics will "continue to favour concentration" versus geographic diversification. Concentration here means clustering production narrowly — the opposite of even, wide distribution.

The gloss fails; concentration means gathering in few places, not spreading evenly.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Below is one short sentence taken directly from the passage. Each numbered option is a paraphrase claiming to preserve its original meaning. Decide whether each one actually does. Original sentence: "Critics counter that this dynamic could equally be read as making Taiwan a uniquely tempting target rather than a uniquely protected one."
statements: Critics argue the same situation might instead make Taiwan especially attractive to attack, not especially safe from it.
Critics agree that this dynamic clearly makes Taiwan the most protected location in the region, with no plausible alternative interpretation.
Critics suggest this dynamic could be interpreted either way, making Taiwan both unusually vulnerable and unusually secure at the same time.
According to critics, the same circumstances might just as easily mark Taiwan out as a prime target as they might mark it out as being shielded.
Critics dismiss the idea that Taiwan's situation carries any strategic risk or protection whatsoever.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Critics argue the same situation might instead make Taiwan especially attractive to attack, not especially safe from it.**

The original says critics counter that the silicon-shield dynamic "could equally be read as making Taiwan a uniquely tempting target rather than a uniquely protected one." "Attractive to attack" ↔ "tempting target" and "not especially safe" ↔ "rather than… protected" preserve that reversal.

The paraphrase keeps the critics' target-not-shielded flip, so it stands.

**B) Critics agree that this dynamic clearly makes Taiwan the most protected location in the region, with no plausible alternative interpretation.**

Critics do not agree with the protective reading; they counter it. "Clearly… most protected" and "no plausible alternative" erase both the countering stance and the "could equally be read" hedge.

**Trap:** Critics' challenge is rewritten as endorsement of the shield.

The paraphrase fails; the original is an alternative reading (tempting target), not critics affirming unique protection.

**C) Critics suggest this dynamic could be interpreted either way, making Taiwan both unusually vulnerable and unusually secure at the same time.**

"Could equally be read as… rather than…" presents the target reading as a rival that displaces the protected reading, not as critics holding both vulnerability and security simultaneously. "Both… at the same time" invents a both/and stance the sentence does not claim.

**Trap:** Rather than (replacement) is misheard as both/and.

The paraphrase fails; critics offer an alternative target reading, not simultaneous dual endorsement.

**D) According to critics, the same circumstances might just as easily mark Taiwan out as a prime target as they might mark it out as being shielded.**

"Might just as easily… as…" restates "could equally be read as… rather than…": same hedge, same target-versus-shielded contrast, without adding certainty or dropping the critics' frame.

The equal-possibility target-vs-shielded wording matches the original, so the paraphrase holds.

**E) Critics dismiss the idea that Taiwan's situation carries any strategic risk or protection whatsoever.**

Critics do not dismiss strategy altogether; they argue the silicon-shield story can be read as greater temptation, not that risk and protection are nonexistent. Total dismissal invents a claim the sentence never makes.

The paraphrase fails; critics reframe the dynamic as a tempting target, they do not deny strategic stakes entirely.
highlights: critics counter that this dynamic could equally be read as making Taiwan a uniquely tempting target rather than a uniquely protected one
critics counter that this dynamic could equally be read as making Taiwan a uniquely tempting target rather than a uniquely protected one
could equally be read as making Taiwan a uniquely tempting target rather than a uniquely protected one
could equally be read as making Taiwan a uniquely tempting target rather than a uniquely protected one
critics counter that this dynamic could equally be read as making Taiwan a uniquely tempting target rather than a uniquely protected one

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in order, with one numeric statement included.
statements: Thwaites Glacier is roughly the size of Great Britain.
Full disintegration would raise sea levels by 65 centimetres.
Retreat slows once warm water reaches inland bedrock.
The glacier's bedrock slopes upward as it moves inland.
Marine ice sheet instability describes a self-reinforcing melting process.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Thwaites Glacier is roughly the size of Great Britain.**

Paragraph 1 opens with a direct size comparison: a glacier "roughly the size of Great Britain" sits in West Antarctica. The statement simply repeats that explicit scale, without adding numbers or geography the text never gives.

**Tip:** Treat bare size or place analogies as true when they echo the passage word-for-word or with a light paraphrase.

The size match is stated outright in Paragraph 1, so the claim is true.

**B) Full disintegration would raise sea levels by 65 centimetres.**

Still in Paragraph 1, the text says that if Thwaites were to "disintegrate entirely, global sea levels would rise by roughly 65 centimetres." The statement's "full disintegration" is just a clean rephrase of that total-collapse scenario, and the centimetre figure is unchanged.

The 65-centimetre rise is the passage's own number for complete loss, so the claim matches.

**C) Retreat slows once warm water reaches inland bedrock.**

Paragraph 2 says the opposite: once retreat begins, warmer water can flow ever deeper beneath the ice, "accelerating melting rather than slowing it." The statement flips that causal direction—from acceleration to slowing—so it fails against the stability mechanism the text names.

**Trap:** Watch for verbs that reverse the marine ice-sheet feedback; the passage insists melt speeds up, not cools down.

The claim reverses Paragraph 2's accelerating feedback, so it fails.

**D) The glacier's bedrock slopes upward as it moves inland.**

Paragraph 2 locates the danger in bedrock that "slopes downward inland," not upward. An upward slope would block warm-water intrusion; a downward one enables the self-reinforcing retreat the paragraph describes. The statement simply swaps the slope direction.

Downward inland, not upward, is the bedrock fact, so the claim is false.

**E) Marine ice sheet instability describes a self-reinforcing melting process.**

Paragraph 2 ends by labelling that self-reinforcing melt loop: "a self-reinforcing process glaciologists call marine ice sheet instability." The statement faithfully restates that definition—name and mechanism line up.

The term and the feedback process are equated in Paragraph 2, so the claim is true.
highlights: a glacier roughly the size of Great Britain
were it to disintegrate entirely, global sea levels would rise by roughly 65 centimetres
accelerating melting rather than slowing it
bedrock that slopes downward inland
a self-reinforcing process glaciologists call marine ice sheet instability

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in order, with one numeric statement included.
statements: The 2019 cavity was roughly two-thirds Manhattan's size.
The cavity once held about 14 billion tonnes of ice.
Surface observations alone had already revealed this cavity's full extent.
Losing the ice shelf's buttress could add three metres of sea-level rise.
That additional rise would unfold within a single decade.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The 2019 cavity was roughly two-thirds Manhattan's size.**

Paragraph 3 reports that in 2019 radar found a cavity "roughly twothirds the size of Manhattan." The statement's hyphenated "two-thirds" is the same fraction; it does not invent a larger or later cavity.

The Manhattan-scale comparison is Paragraph 3's own measure, so the claim is true.

**B) The cavity once held about 14 billion tonnes of ice.**

The same sentence says the cavity was "large enough to have once contained approximately 14 billion tonnes of ice that had already melted away." "About" fairly covers "approximately," and the tonne count is unchanged.

The 14-billion-tonne figure is stated in Paragraph 3, so the claim matches.

**C) Surface observations alone had already revealed this cavity's full extent.**

Paragraph 3 stresses the opposite: warm-water erosion was "far more extensively than surface observations alone had suggested." Radar, not surface surveys, revealed the cavity's scale. The statement credits surface data with a discovery the text withholds from them.

**Trap:** "Already" + surface methods is a common flip—Paragraph 3 says surface data understated the problem.

Surface observations alone missed this extent, so the claim fails.

**D) Losing the ice shelf's buttress could add three metres of sea-level rise.**

Paragraph 4 estimates that if the buttressing effect were entirely lost, surrounding glaciers "could eventually contribute an additional three metres of sea-level rise." The statement correctly ties that three-metre add-on to loss of the ice shelf's buttress role.

The three-metre estimate is Paragraph 4's figure for lost buttressing, so the claim is true.

**E) That additional rise would unfold within a single decade.**

Paragraph 4 immediately times the extra rise as "unfolding over centuries rather than years." A single decade is far shorter than that multi-century window, so the statement invents a rapid timetable the text rejects.

Centuries, not a decade, is the span given, so the claim is false.

approximately 14 billion tonnes of ice
far more extensively than surface observations alone had suggested

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in order, with one numeric statement included.
statements: Since the 1990s, ice loss has roughly doubled.
This acceleration has proceeded smoothly without any pauses.
The joint research collaboration began in 2018.
All model projections agree closely on collapse timing.
Coastal planners currently face a genuinely wide projection range.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Since the 1990s, ice loss has roughly doubled.**

Paragraph 5 reports that satellite measurements show Thwaites "has roughly doubled its rate of ice loss" since the 1990s. The statement repeats that doubling without inventing a steeper surge or a different start year.

The doubled-loss claim is Paragraph 5's own statistic, so it is true.

**B) This acceleration has proceeded smoothly without any pauses.**

The same paragraph cautions that acceleration "has not proceeded smoothly"; sections have "periodically stabilised before resuming retreat." "Without any pauses" erases those temporary stabilisations the text explicitly records.

**Trap:** Doubling overall does not mean a smooth, unbroken climb—Paragraph 5 flags stop-start behaviour.

Pauses and restabilisations contradict "smoothly," so the claim fails.

**C) The joint research collaboration began in 2018.**

Paragraph 6 introduces the International Thwaites Glacier Collaboration as a U.S.–U.K. venture "beginning in 2018." The statement names that start date accurately and invents no earlier founding year.

The 2018 start is stated in Paragraph 6, so the claim is true.

**D) All model projections agree closely on collapse timing.**

Paragraph 7 opens with projections that "remain strikingly divergent"—decades in some runs, centuries in others. "Agree closely" is the exact opposite of that advertised mismatch.

Striking divergence overturns close agreement, so the claim is false.

**E) Coastal planners currently face a genuinely wide projection range.**

Paragraph 8 says current projections "span a range wide enough to make precise, decades-ahead planning genuinely difficult." Coastal engineers, planners, and insurers all work under that spread. The statement's "genuinely wide" tracks the passage's own wording.

The wide projection span for coastal planning is Paragraph 8's point, so the claim matches.
highlights: Since the 1990s, satellite measurements show Thwaites has roughly doubled its rate of ice loss
this acceleration has not proceeded smoothly; certain sections have periodically stabilised
beginning in 2018
Model projections of Thwaites' future remain strikingly divergent

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Statements test whether an inference is actually supported, with one numeric statement included.
statements: Downward-sloping bedrock helps explain accelerating, self-reinforcing retreat.
If loss doubled since the 1990s, retreat has clearly worsened.
Divergent models imply scientists fully agree on collapse timing.
Buttressing loss implies inland glaciers depend partly on Thwaites.
Stabilised sections prove the glacier's overall retreat has ended.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Downward-sloping bedrock helps explain accelerating, self-reinforcing retreat.**

Paragraph 2 links bedrock that "slopes downward inland" to ever-deeper warm water and "accelerating melting," which glaciologists call "marine ice sheet instability." The inference is not a stretch: the slope is offered as the mechanism behind the self-reinforcing speed-up.

The bedrock geometry and the feedback are tied together in Paragraph 2, so the inference holds.

**B) If loss doubled since the 1990s, retreat has clearly worsened.**

Paragraph 5's doubling of the ice-loss rate since the 1990s is already framed as acceleration (even with intermittent pauses). A higher loss rate is a straightforward worsening of retreat intensity relative to that earlier baseline.

**Tip:** "Clearly worsened" here tracks rate of ice loss, not a claim that every section is always retreating at once.

Doubled loss since the 1990s supports a worse retreat rate, so the inference is true.

**C) Divergent models imply scientists fully agree on collapse timing.**

Paragraph 7 calls the projections "strikingly divergent" and traces that gap to uncertainty and hard-to-model ice physics. Divergence is evidence of disagreement about timing, not of "full agree[ment]." The inference flips the logical force of the word.

**Trap:** "Divergent" never licenses unanimous timing; it blocks it.

Divergence contradicts full agreement, so the claim fails.

**D) Buttressing loss implies inland glaciers depend partly on Thwaites.**

Paragraph 4 says Thwaites' ice shelf "holds back a much larger mass of ice further inland," and that losing that buttress could unlock metres of extra rise from surrounding glaciers. Dependence of inland ice on Thwaites' buttress is exactly what that relationship implies.

The inland buttressing role supports partial dependence, so the inference is true.

**E) Stabilised sections prove the glacier's overall retreat has ended.**

Paragraph 5 notes only that certain sections "periodically stabilised before resuming retreat." Temporary pauses before restarting do not prove that overall retreat has ended; they complicate a simple future path while retreat continues.

Stabilisation then "resuming retreat" overturns an "ended" verdict, so the claim is false.
highlights: bedrock that slopes downward inland, meaning that once retreat begins, warmer ocean water can flow ever deeper beneath the ice, accelerating melting rather than slowing it
Thwaites has roughly doubled its rate of ice loss
Model projections of Thwaites' future remain strikingly divergent
its ice shelf currently holds back a much larger mass of ice further inland
certain sections have periodically stabilised before resuming retreat

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Statements require linking details across sections, with one numeric statement included.
statements: The 2019 cavity discovery helps explain the doubled loss rate since the 1990s.
Uncertain projections help explain why coastal planning remains genuinely difficult.
Because collaboration began in 2018, all uncertainty was fully resolved by then.
Buttressing loss and the three-metre estimate both concern ice beyond Thwaites itself.
Bedrock sloping downward is unrelated to the described instability process.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The 2019 cavity discovery helps explain the doubled loss rate since the 1990s.**

Paragraph 3's cavity shows warm water eroding the underside far more than surface clues suggested; Paragraph 5 records roughly doubled ice loss since the 1990s. Linking underside melt revealed in 2019 to that accelerated loss is a fair cross-section synthesis the text invites, even without a single sentence that pairs the two facts.

**Tip:** Synthesis items can join mechanism (basal melt) to trend (doubled loss) when both are in the passage.

Basal erosion and doubled loss fit together, so the synthesis holds.

**B) Uncertain projections help explain why coastal planning remains genuinely difficult.**

Paragraph 7–8 supply the causal chain: strikingly divergent models create wide projection ranges, and Paragraph 8 says that spread makes "precise, decades-ahead planning genuinely difficult" for coastal work. The statement restates the passage's own bridge from uncertainty to planning trouble.

Wide, uncertain projections are Paragraph 8's reason for planning difficulty, so the claim is true.

**C) Because collaboration began in 2018, all uncertainty was fully resolved by then.**

Paragraph 6 dates the collaboration to 2018; Paragraphs 7–9 still present divergent models and an open question about Thwaites' hazard. Launching research does not mean uncertainty vanished that year—the later paragraphs prove it remains.

**Trap:** A start date is not a resolution date; later paragraphs keep the unknowns alive.

Ongoing divergent projections overturn "fully resolved by 2018," so the claim fails.

**D) Buttressing loss and the three-metre estimate both concern ice beyond Thwaites itself.**

Paragraph 4's buttress holds back "a much larger mass of ice further inland," and the three metres come from "surrounding glaciers" if that effect is lost. Both details point past Thwaites' own ice to the inland system it pins in place.

Inland ice and surrounding glaciers are beyond Thwaites alone, so the synthesis is true.

**E) Bedrock sloping downward is unrelated to the described instability process.**

Paragraph 2 presents downward-sloping bedrock as the setup that lets warm water deepen the retreat and feed "marine ice sheet instability." Calling the slope "unrelated" severs the mechanism the paragraph exists to explain.

The slope is the instability's geometric cause, so the claim is false.
